aqidah.s: The set of things a Muslim holds to be true, as opposed to the things a Muslim does.
aqidah.l: The root means to tie a knot, so aqidah is what the heart is tied to and does not untie. It covers Allah, His angels, His books, His messengers, the Last Day, and the decree. Fiqh answers what you do; aqidah answers what you hold true.

tawhid.s: The belief that Allah is one, without partner, without equal, and alone deserving of worship.
tawhid.l: The word means to make one, or to declare one. Surah al-Ikhlas states it in four short lines: He is One, the Eternal Refuge, He does not beget and was not begotten, and there is nothing comparable to Him (Qur'an 112). Tawhid is not only the claim that one God exists. It is that only He is worshipped.

tawhid-al-rububiyyah.s: Oneness of lordship: that Allah alone creates, owns, sustains and controls everything that exists.
tawhid-al-rububiyyah.l: This is the belief that there is one Creator running one universe, and the Qur'an notes that even the idolaters of Makkah admitted this much when asked who made the heavens and the earth. That is why it is not, by itself, enough to make someone a Muslim. The three part division of tawhid is a teaching framework, used widely since Ibn Taymiyyah; some scholars prefer a two part arrangement, and the difference is about how to teach it rather than what is true.

tawhid-al-uluhiyyah.s: Oneness of worship: that prayer, vows, sacrifice, hope and fear are directed to Allah alone.
tawhid-al-uluhiyyah.l: This is the part the messengers were sent with, and the part people have always argued over. To believe Allah made you is one thing; to bring every act of worship to Him and to no one else is another. Its exact opposite is shirk.

asma-wa-sifat.s: Allah's names and attributes, affirmed as He described them, without denial and without resemblance to creation.
asma-wa-sifat.l: The Qur'an gives Allah names and describes Him with attributes, and it also says there is nothing like Him (Qur'an 42:11). Sunni theology holds both halves at once: affirm what He said about Himself, and do not picture it as a larger version of something created. How far to explain the more difficult descriptions is exactly where the Sunni schools of creed part company.

istiwa.s: The Qur'anic statement that Allah rose over the Throne, and the classic test case for reading divine attributes.
istiwa.l: The Qur'an says the Most Merciful rose over the Throne (Qur'an 20:5). Atharis affirm the wording and leave the manner to Allah, quoting Imam Malik: the rising is known, the how is unknown, and asking about it is an innovation. Many Ash'aris and Maturidis read it as dominion and authority, to keep any bodily picture away. All three agree that Allah is not contained by a place.

tashbih.s: Likening Allah to His creation, which the Qur'an rules out with the words: there is nothing like Him.
tashbih.l: Tashbih is imagining Allah as a bigger, stronger version of something you have already seen. Its mirror error is ta'til, emptying His names and attributes of any real meaning. Sunni creed walks between the two: He is real, He is described, and He is not comparable (Qur'an 42:11).

tafwid.s: Leaving the meaning of a difficult divine attribute to Allah, as opposed to interpreting it figuratively.
tafwid.l: When the texts describe Allah with a hand, a face, or a rising, scholars took two broad roads. Tafwid affirms the word and consigns its reality to Allah without explaining it. Ta'wil interprets it within what the Arabic allows, such as hand meaning power. Atharis lean to the first and Ash'aris and Maturidis often to the second, and each counts the other as Sunni.

ruyat-allah.s: The belief that the people of Paradise will see their Lord with their eyes, after death.
ruyat-allah.l: The Qur'an says that on that Day some faces will be radiant, looking at their Lord (Qur'an 75:22-23), and sound hadiths compare the sight to seeing the full moon without crowding. Sunni Islam affirms this sight in the next life while denying that anyone sees Allah in this one. The Mu'tazila denied it altogether, and Twelver Shia theology also generally rejects a literal vision.

shirk.s: Giving to something other than Allah what belongs to Allah alone, above all worship.
shirk.l: The word means to make a partner or to share. The Qur'an says Allah does not forgive that a partner be set up with Him, and forgives what is less than that for whom He wills (Qur'an 4:48). Commentators read that of the one who dies without repenting, since the Qur'an elsewhere promises forgiveness to whoever turns back. Scholars distinguish major shirk, which takes a person outside Islam, from minor shirk, which is a grave sin but does not.

shirk-asghar.s: Minor shirk: acts like showing off in worship, which damage sincerity without putting a person outside Islam.
shirk-asghar.l: The Prophet peace be upon him called showing off the lesser shirk, in a report collected by Imam Ahmad. Swearing by other than Allah, and saying what Allah and so and so willed, belong to the same family. The point is not to make a believer anxious about every sentence, but to keep worship pointed in one direction.

kufr.s: Disbelief: rejecting or refusing what a person knows Allah has revealed.
kufr.l: The root means to cover, the way a farmer covers a seed with soil, so kufr is covering a truth that has already reached you. Scholars separate major kufr, which places someone outside Islam, from the lesser kufr that some texts use for serious sins committed by a believer. Deciding that a particular person is a disbeliever is a scholarly and judicial matter, not a conversational one.

nifaq.s: Hypocrisy: showing belief outwardly while concealing disbelief, or acting against the faith one claims.
nifaq.l: The Qur'an gives the munafiqun a surah of their own and says the hypocrites will be in the lowest depth of the Fire (Qur'an 4:145). Scholars distinguish nifaq of belief, which is disbelief in disguise, from nifaq of conduct: the well known signs of lying, breaking a promise, and betraying a trust, reported in Bukhari and Muslim. The second kind was taught as a mirror for the believer to check himself, not as a label to hand to others.

takfir.s: Declaring a specific Muslim to be a disbeliever, a ruling classical scholars fenced with heavy conditions.
takfir.l: Scholarship treats takfir as a judgement with conditions and impediments: ignorance, misreading, compulsion, and the absence of clear proof all block it. The Prophet peace be upon him warned that when a man calls his brother a disbeliever it returns to one of the two, in a report in Bukhari and Muslim. Saying that a statement is disbelief is not the same as saying the person who said it is a disbeliever, and the second was left to qualified scholars.

iman.s: Faith: belief in Allah, His angels, His books, His messengers, the Last Day, and the decree.
iman.l: The six articles come from the hadith of Jibril in Sahih Muslim, where the angel asks the Prophet peace be upon him what faith is and then confirms his answer. Iman is more than agreement in the mind; the texts tie it to the tongue and to the limbs as well. Most Sunni scholars hold that iman increases and decreases, while the Hanafi and Maturidi tradition holds that its essence stays fixed even as its light grows.

islam.s: Submission to Allah: outwardly the five pillars, inwardly the handing over of the whole self.
islam.l: The word comes from a root carrying both surrender and peace, and the Qur'an calls it the religion with Allah (Qur'an 3:19). In the hadith of Jibril, islam is answered with the five pillars, iman with the six articles of belief, and ihsan with the quality of worship. So islam is the outward frame, iman the inner conviction, and ihsan the finish on both.

ihsan.s: To worship Allah as though you see Him, and if you do not see Him, knowing that He sees you.
ihsan.l: The definition is the Prophet's own wording in the hadith of Jibril, collected in Bukhari and Muslim. The word means to do a thing beautifully, and it reaches past worship into how a person treats people and animals. It is the difference between a prayer performed and a prayer attended.

arkan-al-iman.s: The six articles of faith: Allah, His angels, His books, His messengers, the Last Day, and the decree.
arkan-al-iman.l: They are listed together in the hadith of Jibril, recorded in Sahih Muslim, when the Prophet peace be upon him is asked what faith is. The Qur'an gathers most of them in a single verse about the believers (Qur'an 2:285). These six are the frame, and almost every other question of creed is a detail hanging inside one of them.

fitrah.s: The natural disposition every person is born with, leaning toward recognising one Creator.
fitrah.l: The Qur'an speaks of the fitrah of Allah upon which He made people (Qur'an 30:30), and the Prophet peace be upon him said that every child is born upon the fitrah, in Bukhari and Muslim. It is not a memory of doctrine but a leaning, and it is easily covered over by habit and upbringing. In fiqh the same word names the acts of natural cleanliness, which is a separate meaning of one root.

qadr.s: Allah's decree: that He knows, wrote, willed and created all that happens, without forcing anyone to sin.
qadr.l: Scholars describe four levels to it: Allah's knowledge of everything, its writing in the Preserved Tablet, His will, and His creating it. The Qur'an says He created every thing in due measure (Qur'an 54:49), and the word itself carries measure rather than blind fate. Belief in qadr is the sixth article of faith in the hadith of Jibril. It does not remove your choice and it is not a reason to stop trying, which is why the Prophet peace be upon him answered a question about it by telling the man to act.

qada.s: Allah's decree carried out: the partner word to qadr, though scholars differ over which term means which.
qada.l: One common explanation is that qadr is the eternal measuring and qada is the putting into effect, while other scholars reverse the two. Either way, when the pair is used together they mean one thing: nothing reaches you from outside Allah's knowledge and will. In fiqh the same word means making up a missed prayer or fast, and it also means a judge's ruling, which are different uses of one root.

ikhtiyar.s: Human choice: real enough to be answerable for, and never outside Allah's knowledge and creation.
ikhtiyar.l: Two old errors sit on either side of the road. The Jabriyyah said a person is compelled, like a feather in wind; the Qadariyyah said a person creates his own acts independently of Allah's decree. Ahl al-Sunnah hold both truths together: Allah creates the act, and the servant genuinely chooses and earns it, a position the Ash'aris call kasb.

ajal.s: The appointed term of a life or a nation, which does not arrive early or run late.
ajal.l: The Qur'an says that when their term comes they cannot delay it by an hour, nor bring it forward (Qur'an 7:34). It is why a believer can take medicine and take cover without any contradiction: means are commanded, outcomes are decreed. The reports that keeping ties of kinship lengthens a life are explained as blessing placed in the time given, or as what stands in the angels' record rather than in Allah's knowledge.

al-ghayb.s: Everything real that lies beyond the reach of the senses, known only because Allah reported it.
al-ghayb.l: The Qur'an opens by describing the God fearing as those who believe in the unseen (Qur'an 2:3). It covers Allah Himself, the angels, the jinn, the grave, the Day of Judgement, Paradise and the Fire. Scholars call these matters sam'iyyat, things received by report, because reason can accept them but could never have discovered them. Claiming private access to the unseen, through stars or cards or spirits, is claiming something the Qur'an reserves to Allah.

wahy.s: Revelation: Allah's speech conveyed to a prophet, directly, from behind a veil, or through an angel.
wahy.l: The Qur'an describes exactly those three modes (Qur'an 42:51), and says the Prophet peace be upon him did not speak from desire, but that it was revelation revealed (Qur'an 53:3-4). Revelation of this kind came to prophets only, and it ended with the death of the last of them. Nothing after him, however sincere or however true it feels, carries the same authority. Where the Qur'an uses the same verb of the bee or of the mother of Musa, scholars read inspiration rather than prophecy.

ilham.s: Inspiration placed in a heart, which may be true but is not revelation and is not proof for anyone else.
ilham.l: The Qur'an uses the word for the soul being inspired with its wrong and its right (Qur'an 91:8). Sunni scholars accept that a righteous person may be given true insight, and still refuse to build a ruling on it, because ilham is not protected from error. If an inspiration contradicts the Qur'an or the Sunnah it is set aside without argument. Sufi writing uses kashf, unveiling, for a similar idea, under the same rule.

nubuwwah.s: Prophethood: Allah choosing certain men to receive revelation and deliver it, ending with Muhammad, peace be upon him.
nubuwwah.l: The Qur'an names many prophets and says every nation was sent a warner. A rasul is usually described as one sent with a new law or to a rejecting people, and a nabi as one continuing a law already given, though scholars word the distinction in different ways. Prophets are protected in conveying the message, a quality called ismah. Muhammad peace be upon him is the seal of them, so no prophet comes after him (Qur'an 33:40).

kutub.s: The scriptures Allah revealed, belief in them being one of the six articles of faith.
kutub.l: A Muslim believes that Allah spoke to earlier communities and that those revelations were true when they were given (Qur'an 2:285). The Qur'an names the Tawrat given to Musa, the Zabur to Dawud, the Injil to Isa, and pages given to Ibrahim and Musa. The mainstream position is that earlier scriptures were altered in wording or in handling over time, so present copies are not taken as authority, while the Qur'an is held to be the final one and preserved.

mujizah.s: A miracle given to a prophet as proof of prophethood, which his opponents are unable to match.
mujizah.l: The word means that which renders others powerless. The staff of Musa, the healing given to Isa, and the splitting of the moon are examples, and the standing miracle of Muhammad peace be upon him is the Qur'an itself. A mu'jizah is public, tied to a claim of prophethood, and impossible to imitate, and that is what separates it from a karamah.

karamah.s: An extraordinary event granted to a righteous believer, with no claim to prophethood attached.
karamah.l: Ahl al-Sunnah affirm karamat, pointing to Maryam finding provision out of season (Qur'an 3:37) and to the sleepers of the cave. The Mu'tazila denied them. Sunni scholars then set one plain rule: a person's uprightness on the Sunnah is the proof, not the wonder, so someone who breaks the sacred law while performing marvels is not a friend of Allah but a warning.

istidraj.s: Being drawn in slowly by blessings while sinning, so that ease becomes a punishment rather than approval.
istidraj.l: The Qur'an says of those who deny its signs: We will lead them on by degrees from where they do not know (Qur'an 7:182). It is the answer to a question people ask honestly, which is why the wrongdoer prospers. Comfort is not a verdict, and neither is hardship.

ruh.s: The spirit that gives a body life, whose reality Allah kept to Himself.
ruh.l: When the Prophet peace be upon him was asked about the ruh, the answer came: say, the spirit is from the affair of my Lord, and you have been given only a little knowledge (Qur'an 17:85). It is taken at death, held in the barzakh, and returned to the body at the resurrection. Many scholars use ruh and nafs for the same thing seen from two angles, while others treat them as distinct.

nafs.s: The self: the inner person that can command wrong, blame itself, or come to rest.
nafs.l: The Qur'an describes it in three states: the soul that commands evil (Qur'an 12:53), the self reproaching soul (Qur'an 75:2), and the soul at peace, called back to its Lord well pleased (Qur'an 89:27-28). These are not three souls but one self in three conditions, and a person moves between them in a single day. Struggling with the nafs is ordinary religious life, not a sign that something has gone wrong.

malaikah.s: Angels: beings created from light who never disobey Allah and carry out exactly what they are commanded.
malaikah.l: Belief in them is one of the six articles of faith. Their creation from light is reported in Sahih Muslim rather than in the Qur'an. They are not male or female in the human sense, they do not eat or tire, and the Qur'an says they do not disobey Allah in what He commands them and do what they are told (Qur'an 66:6). A few are named in the texts, most are not, and their number is known to Allah alone.

kiraman-katibin.s: The two honourable scribes who record what every person says and does.
kiraman-katibin.l: The Qur'an says over you are keepers, noble writers, who know what you do (Qur'an 82:10-12), and that not a word is uttered without a watcher ready beside him (Qur'an 50:18). The names Raqib and Atid come from reading two words of that verse as names rather than as descriptions. What they write becomes the record handed to each person on the Day of Judgement, a book that leaves out nothing small or large (Qur'an 18:49). The verses were given to produce attention rather than dread.

munkar-wa-nakir.s: The two angels who question a person in the grave about their Lord, their religion, and their prophet.
munkar-wa-nakir.l: They are named in a hadith reported by al-Tirmidhi, and the three questions appear in several sound narrations. The believer answers with certainty and the grave is widened for him; the one who lived heedless can only say that he heard people saying something and repeated it. This is the trial of the grave that the Prophet peace be upon him taught his companions to seek refuge from in every prayer.

malak-al-mawt.s: The angel of death, who takes each soul at its appointed time by Allah's command.
malak-al-mawt.l: The Qur'an says: the angel of death, who has been put in charge of you, will take you, then to your Lord you will be returned (Qur'an 32:11). The name Izra'il is widely used but does not come from the Qur'an or from an authentic hadith, where he is simply called the angel of death. Narrations describe helpers who assist him in taking souls.

jinn.s: A created race made from fire, unseen to us, who like people believe or disbelieve and are accountable.
jinn.l: The Qur'an gives them a surah of their own (Qur'an 72), reports a group of them listening to the recitation and accepting it, and says they were created from a smokeless flame of fire (Qur'an 55:15). They eat, they marry, they die, and they will be judged. They are not the spirits of dead humans, and they are not behind most of what gets blamed on them.

iblis.s: The jinn who refused to prostrate to Adam out of pride, and was expelled and granted respite.
iblis.l: The Qur'an tells the scene several times and states plainly that he was of the jinn, and so he departed from the command of his Lord (Qur'an 18:50). He asked for time until the Day they are raised and was given it. Iblis is his name, while shaytan describes what he became, and what his followers among jinn and men are called.

shaytan.s: A devil: any rebellious jinn, and with the definite article, Iblis himself.
shaytan.l: The Qur'an says he is an enemy to you, so take him as an enemy (Qur'an 35:6), and gives him only two tools, whispering and inviting. He cannot compel anyone; on the Day of Judgement he tells his own followers that he had no authority over them except that he called and they answered (Qur'an 14:22). The Qur'an also calls some human beings shayatin, so the word is not limited to jinn.

qarin.s: The jinn companion assigned to each person, whose work is whispering toward wrong.
qarin.l: The Prophet peace be upon him said that every one of you has a companion from the jinn and a companion from the angels, in a report in Sahih Muslim, and said that his own had submitted so that it only urged him toward good. The Qur'an uses the same word for a companion who speaks up on the Day of Judgement (Qur'an 50:23-27). It is not a double of you, a shadow self, or a source of information about your life, and most of the popular material about it goes far beyond anything the texts say.

barzakh.s: The state between death and the resurrection, where the soul waits after the body is buried.
barzakh.l: The word means a barrier or partition. The Qur'an uses it of the one who begs to be returned to life and is refused: behind them is a barrier until the Day they are raised (Qur'an 23:100). It is a real condition, with ease or with distress, and its details are not measurable by anything we can observe from this side.

adhab-al-qabr.s: The punishment or ease a person meets in the grave, before the Day of Judgement arrives.
adhab-al-qabr.l: The Qur'an describes the people of Fir'awn exposed to the Fire morning and evening before the Hour comes (Qur'an 40:46), and many sound hadiths describe the grave as either a garden of Paradise or a pit of the Fire. Ahl al-Sunnah affirm it as real without claiming to know how it works upon a body that has decayed or was never buried. The Mu'tazila denied it; the Sunni schools do not.

qiyamah.s: The Day of Resurrection, when this creation ends, the dead are raised, and everyone is judged.
qiyamah.l: The word means the standing, because people stand before their Lord. Its timing is known to Allah alone, though the Prophet peace be upon him described signs that come before it. The Qur'an returns to this Day constantly, not to frighten, but because a life that ends in an account is lived differently from one that does not.

ashrat-al-saah.s: The signs that come before the Day of Judgement, sorted by scholars into minor and major.
ashrat-al-saah.l: The Qur'an says its signs have already come (Qur'an 47:18), which commentators read as the sending of the final Prophet. The minor signs are gradual changes in society described across the hadith literature; the major ones are the ten listed in a report in Sahih Muslim, among them the Dajjal, the descent of Isa, Ya'juj and Ma'juj, the beast, the smoke, the sun rising from the west, and a fire that drives people to their final gathering. Reading current events as the fulfilment of signs is an old habit, and every attempt to put a date on it has been wrong so far.

dajjal.s: The false messiah who appears near the end of time, claiming godhood and testing people with power.
dajjal.l: He is not named in the Qur'an, but the reports about him are so numerous that Sunni scholars treat them as certain. He is described as one eyed, with disbelief written between his eyes, given power to show wonders and to control provision, and finally killed by Isa. The Prophet peace be upon him said that every prophet warned his people about him, and taught the opening verses of Surah al-Kahf as protection.

mahdi.s: A rightly guided leader expected near the end of time, understood very differently by Sunni and Shia Islam.
mahdi.l: In Sunni Islam he is a future man from the family of the Prophet peace be upon him who will rule with justice, described in reports collected by Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi and others; most scholars accepted them, while a minority, including Ibn Khaldun, criticised their chains. He is not named in the Qur'an. Twelver Shia belief is different in kind: the Mahdi there is the twelfth Imam, already born, alive in occultation, and awaited. Claimants have appeared in almost every century, and each one so far has been mistaken.

nuzul-isa.s: The descent of Isa near the end of time, to break the cross, kill the Dajjal, and rule with justice.
nuzul-isa.l: The Qur'an says he was not killed and not crucified, but that Allah raised him (Qur'an 4:157-158), and calls him a sign of the Hour (Qur'an 43:61). The hadiths describe his descent, his prayer behind the leader of the Muslims, and his death and burial afterwards like any other human being. He returns as a follower of the final Prophet, not with a new religion.

yajuj-wa-majuj.s: Two peoples held back behind a barrier built by Dhu al-Qarnayn, released as a major sign of the Hour.
yajuj-wa-majuj.l: The Qur'an tells the story of the barrier of iron and molten copper (Qur'an 18:94-98) and says that when they are released they will swarm down from every height (Qur'an 21:96). Scholars have guessed for centuries about who and where they are; the honest answer is that the texts describe a time, not a place on a map. Their release is one of the ten major signs.

sur.s: The horn that is blown to end this world, and blown again to raise the dead.
sur.l: The Qur'an says the horn is blown and everyone in the heavens and the earth falls dead except whom Allah wills, then it is blown a second time and they are standing, looking on (Qur'an 39:68). The angel entrusted with it is named Israfil in the hadith literature. Reports describe him holding it to his mouth, head inclined, waiting for the command.

bath.s: The resurrection: bodies raised and souls returned, so that everyone stands for judgement.
bath.l: The Qur'an answers the objection directly, asking who will give life to bones after they have crumbled, and replying that He who produced them the first time will (Qur'an 36:78-79). The gathering that follows is called the hashr, on an open plain where nobody is missed or overlooked. Sunni belief is that the raising is bodily and not only spiritual.

hisab.s: The reckoning: each person shown their record and questioned about the life they were given.
hisab.l: The Qur'an describes books handed to the right hand and to the left, and an easy reckoning for some (Qur'an 84:7-9). The Prophet peace be upon him said that a servant's feet will not move on that Day until he is asked about his life, his knowledge, his wealth and his body, in a report collected by al-Tirmidhi. Sound narrations also describe a group entering Paradise with no reckoning at all.

sahifah.s: The record of a person's deeds, handed to them on the Day of Judgement.
sahifah.l: The Qur'an says every person's record is fastened to them and will be brought out as a book found spread open, with the words: read your record, today you are sufficient as a reckoner against yourself (Qur'an 17:13-14). Elsewhere the wrongdoers say of it: what kind of book is this, it leaves out nothing small or large (Qur'an 18:49). Receiving it in the right hand is the sign of success.

mizan.s: The scale on which deeds are weighed on the Day of Judgement, with exact justice.
mizan.l: The Qur'an says the scales of justice will be set up for the Day of Resurrection, so that no soul is wronged in anything, even the weight of a mustard seed (Qur'an 21:47). Sunni belief takes this as a real scale and not only a figure of speech. Some small deeds are described as heavy upon it, far out of proportion to the effort they cost, which is worth remembering.

sirat.s: The bridge laid over Hell that everyone must cross, at speeds matching their deeds.
sirat.l: It is described in the long hadith of intercession in Bukhari and Muslim: people pass over it like lightning, like the wind, like a running horse, or crawling, and some are seized along the way. The Qur'an speaks of every one of you coming to it (Qur'an 19:71), which many commentators read as this crossing. The same word in Surah al-Fatihah means the straight path in this life, a different sense of one root.

hawd.s: The Prophet's pool, where his community drinks before entering Paradise and never thirsts again.
hawd.l: The narrations about it are numerous and agreed upon: its water whiter than milk, sweeter than honey, its cups like the stars of the sky. The Prophet peace be upon him said he will be at it ahead of his community, and that some who belonged to him will be turned away for what they introduced after him. Al-Kawthar, the river given to him in Paradise (Qur'an 108:1), is described in the reports as feeding it.

shafaah.s: Intercession: one person asking Allah on behalf of another, and only by Allah's permission.
shafaah.l: The Qur'an denies intercession that works like influence over a king, and affirms it with permission: who is there that can intercede with Him except by His leave (Qur'an 2:255). The greatest instance is the Maqam Mahmud, the praised station, where the Prophet peace be upon him asks for the standing to be relieved and the judgement to begin. Angels, prophets, martyrs and even a person's own children are described as interceding. Asking Allah to grant you the Prophet's intercession is agreed upon; addressing the deceased directly is where positions divide.

jannah.s: Paradise: the garden of lasting delight prepared for the believers, where nothing is lost or spoiled.
jannah.l: The word means a garden covered over by its own foliage, and the Qur'an describes rivers, shade and gardens, then says the pleasure of Allah is greater than all of it (Qur'an 9:72). A sacred hadith describes what is in it as what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and no heart has imagined. Firdaws is named as its highest part, beneath the Throne. In Sunni belief its greatest gift is the sight of Allah Himself.

jahannam.s: The Fire: the punishment prepared for those who refused, described in the Qur'an in plain and heavy terms.
jahannam.l: The Qur'an gives it names and levels and says the Fire was prepared for those who reject faith (Qur'an 2:24). Sunni belief holds that believers who enter it for their sins do not remain in it, and are brought out by mercy and intercession, while disbelief carried to the grave meets a lasting punishment. The verses are not decoration, and they are also not an invitation to guess who is going there.

akhirah.s: The hereafter: everything after death, from the grave to the final settling in Paradise or the Fire.
akhirah.l: The Qur'an pairs it constantly with the dunya, the near life, and says the hereafter is better and more lasting (Qur'an 87:17). Belief in it is one of the six articles of faith. It is not an escape from this world; the same Qur'an teaches the believer to ask for good in both.

sunnah.s: The Prophet's way in belief, worship and conduct, and the measure against which innovation is judged.
sunnah.l: The word means a trodden path. In hadith study it covers what the Prophet peace be upon him said, did, and quietly approved; in fiqh it also names a recommended act; in creed it means the received way of the first generations, which is why the phrase Ahl al-Sunnah exists. Set against bid'ah, sunnah means the shape of the religion as it was handed over, rather than anyone's personal preference.

bidah.s: Innovation in religion: introducing an act of worship that has no basis in what was revealed.
bidah.l: The Prophet peace be upon him said that whoever introduces into this affair of ours something that is not from it will have it rejected, in Bukhari and Muslim. Everyone agrees that new things in worldly life are not the subject; nobody calls a printing press or a microphone bid'ah. Scholars differ on the categories: many, following al-Shafi'i and al-Izz ibn Abd al-Salam, sort innovations into praiseworthy and blameworthy, while others hold that whatever is correctly called bid'ah in religion is blameworthy, and the good cases were never bid'ah to begin with.

ahl-al-sunnah.s: The main body of Muslims who follow the Prophet's way and the practice of his companions.
ahl-al-sunnah.l: The name joins two things: the sunnah, and the jama'ah, the community that held to it. In creed the Sunni world recognises three schools, Ash'ari, Maturidi and Athari; in law it recognises four, Hanafi, Maliki, Shafi'i and Hanbali. Difference inside those boundaries is old and normal, and is not the same thing as stepping outside them.

ashari.s: A Sunni school of creed founded by Abu al-Hasan al-Ash'ari, defending orthodox belief with reasoned argument.
ashari.l: Al-Ash'ari trained among the Mu'tazila and then left them, turning their own methods toward defending the positions of the people of hadith. The school became associated with Shafi'i and Maliki scholarship, and with figures such as al-Ghazali, al-Razi and al-Nawawi. On the difficult attribute verses it tends toward interpretation or consignment rather than literal wording. It is one of the three creed schools recognised within Ahl al-Sunnah.

maturidi.s: A Sunni school of creed founded by Abu Mansur al-Maturidi, closely tied to the Hanafi tradition.
maturidi.l: It grew in Samarqand and became the creed of most Hanafis, and so of much of Turkey, Central Asia, and the Indian subcontinent. It stands close to the Ash'ari school and differs on a set of fine points, such as how far reason alone can establish that Allah must be known before revelation arrives, and whether iman itself increases and decreases. Each school counts the other as Sunni.

athari.s: The Sunni creed school that keeps to the wording of the texts and avoids theological speculation.
athari.l: Athar means a narration, and the approach is to affirm what the Qur'an and Sunnah say about Allah in their own words, without figurative interpretation and without asking how. It is associated with Ahmad ibn Hanbal, and later with Ibn Taymiyyah and with much modern Salafi thought. Along with the Ash'aris and Maturidis it is one of the three recognised Sunni creed schools, and the argument between the three is old, sharp, and internal.

tawassul.s: Approaching Allah through a means, such as His names, your own good deeds, or a living person's du'a.
tawassul.l: All schools agree on three forms: by Allah's names and attributes, by your own righteous deeds, and by asking a living righteous person to pray for you, the last shown in the hadith of the blind man and in Umar asking al-Abbas to pray for rain. They differ over tawassul by the person or rank of a prophet or saint, especially after death. Many Hanafi, Maliki, Shafi'i and Sufi scholars permit it as a form of asking Allah, while Hanbali and Salafi scholarship generally rejects it as a door to worse. All sides agree that asking the dead to grant something themselves is not tawassul at all but shirk.

wasilah.s: A means of nearness to Allah, and also the name of a specific high station in Paradise.
wasilah.l: The Qur'an commands: seek the means of nearness to Him (Qur'an 5:35), which the commentators explain as obedience and whatever brings a servant close. The word is also the name of a rank in Paradise which the Prophet peace be upon him said belongs to one servant only, and which he taught his community to ask for on his behalf after the call to prayer. The two meanings share a root and are often mixed up in argument.

istighathah.s: Calling for help, and the disputed question of whom a Muslim may call on when it is not Allah.
istighathah.l: Everyone agrees that asking a present living person for help within their ability is ordinary and permitted, and that asking anyone at all for what only Allah can give is shirk. The dispute is narrower than it sounds: calling on an absent or deceased prophet or righteous person. Many Sufi and traditional scholars read it as a request for that person's prayer and permit it, while Hanbali and Salafi scholarship reads it as calling upon the dead and forbids it. Both sides are arguing over the meaning of one line said seventeen times a day: You alone we worship, You alone we ask for help (Qur'an 1:5).

arsh.s: The Throne of Allah, the greatest created thing, above the heavens and carried by angels.
arsh.l: The Qur'an says His Throne was upon the water before the heavens and the earth were made (Qur'an 11:7), and describes angels carrying it and surrounding it with praise (Qur'an 40:7). Sunni scholars affirm it as a real created thing and warn against imagining that Allah needs it or is contained by it. The Prophet peace be upon him said that al-Firdaws, the highest part of Paradise, lies directly beneath it.

kursi.s: Something vast that extends over the heavens and the earth, which most scholars hold is distinct from the Throne.
kursi.l: The Qur'an says His Kursi extends over the heavens and the earth, and preserving them does not tire Him (Qur'an 2:255). Ibn Abbas is reported to have explained it as the place of the two feet, while others read it as His knowledge or His dominion. A narration compares the seven heavens beside the Kursi to a ring thrown into open desert, and the Kursi beside the Throne in the same way.

lawh-mahfuz.s: The Preserved Tablet, in which everything decreed was written down before it happened.
lawh-mahfuz.l: The Qur'an closes Surah al-Buruj by calling it a glorious Qur'an in a Preserved Tablet (Qur'an 85:21-22), and speaks elsewhere of the Mother of the Book (Qur'an 43:4). It is the writing stage of the decree: what is in it does not change, and what a person can still change is himself. Its reality belongs to the unseen, so speculation about its material or its size is empty.

qalam.s: The Pen, commanded to write the decree of everything that would happen until the Day of Judgement.
qalam.l: Allah swears by the pen and by what they write (Qur'an 68:1). A hadith in the collections of Abu Dawud and al-Tirmidhi reports that the first thing Allah created was the Pen, and He said to it write, and it wrote what would be until the Hour. The image is not ink and paper but a matter already settled, which is why the Prophet peace be upon him told Ibn Abbas that the pens have been lifted and the pages have dried.

sidrat-al-muntaha.s: The Lote Tree at the furthest limit, reached by the Prophet on the Night Journey.
sidrat-al-muntaha.l: The Qur'an says he saw him at a second descent, by the Lote Tree of the utmost boundary, near which is the Garden of Refuge (Qur'an 53:13-15). Scholars describe it as the boundary past which the knowledge of creation does not go, so it marks a limit rather than a location. It appears in the accounts of the Night Journey, at the stage where the five daily prayers were given.

ahl-al-fatrah.s: People who lived without a prophet's message reaching them, and the question of how they are judged.
ahl-al-fatrah.l: The Qur'an says We do not punish until We have sent a messenger (Qur'an 17:15), which every school takes as the starting point. The Ash'ari position is that such a person is not punished, because obligation begins when the message arrives, while Maturidis hold that reason alone still obliges a person to recognise the Creator. A well known group of hadiths describes them being tested on the Day of Judgement itself, and many scholars, including within the Hanbali tradition, hold that view. What all sides agree on is that these are cases for Allah to judge, and not a category for living people to sort each other into.

shahadah.s: The testimony that there is no god but Allah and that Muhammad is His Messenger.
shahadah.l: It is the first of the five pillars and the door into Islam: whoever says it, understanding and meaning it, is a Muslim. It has two halves, which is why it is often called the shahadatain, the two testimonies. The first half empties the heart of every other object of worship; the second names the one man whose example shows how that worship is done. It is not a formula that works by sound. The scholars set conditions for it, among them knowledge of what it means, certainty rather than doubt, sincerity, truthfulness, love, acceptance and acting on it.

laylat-al-qadr.s: The night in Ramadan that the Qur'an calls better than a thousand months.
laylat-al-qadr.l: A whole surah is named for it, and it says worship in that one night is better than a thousand months, which is more than eighty years. It is sought in the last ten nights of Ramadan, and most strongly in the odd ones, with the twenty seventh most commonly named; the Prophet peace be upon him said to seek it rather than announced it, and the scholars read that hiding as mercy, so that the whole ten are revived. The du'a taught for it asks Allah, who loves to pardon, for pardon.

aqiqah.s: The sacrifice offered for a newborn, customarily on the seventh day, with the naming and the shaving of the head.
aqiqah.l: The reports name two sheep for a boy and one for a girl, and the majority treat it as a strong sunnah rather than an obligation; the Zahiris held it obligatory. It is done on the seventh day where that is possible, and it is not invalid later. The head is shaved and something is given in charity, and the child is named. Nothing in it requires expense a family does not have, and a family that cannot afford it owes nothing.

udhiyah.s: The animal sacrificed on Eid al-Adha and the days after it, in remembrance of Ibrahim.
udhiyah.l: It is offered after the Eid prayer on the tenth of Dhul Hijjah and through the days of tashriq. The Hanafis hold it obligatory on whoever has the means; the other three schools call it a confirmed sunnah. The meat is customarily divided in three, for the household, for relatives and neighbours, and for the poor, though that division is a practice rather than a fixed ruling. It is not the same as the hady, the sacrifice a pilgrim offers as part of Hajj.

kalam-allah.s: The speech of Allah, and the classical controversy over whether the Qur'an is created or uncreated.
kalam-allah.l: The Qur'an is the speech of Allah, and the question the third century argued over was whether that speech is created like everything else or an eternal attribute of the One who speaks. The Mu'tazila held it created; Ahmad ibn Hanbal was imprisoned and beaten under the mihna for refusing to say so, and the position that prevailed in Sunni Islam is that the Qur'an is the uncreated speech of Allah, though the schools word the relation between the eternal attribute and the recited letters differently. It is the clearest case in the tradition of a doctrine settled by somebody's endurance rather than by an argument.

fiqh.s: The human effort to work out Islamic law from its sources, and the rulings that result.
fiqh.l: The word means understanding. Fiqh is not the same as shari'ah: shari'ah is the guidance God revealed, fiqh is what scholars understood of it, which is why qualified people reach different answers. Books of fiqh nearly all run in the same order: purification and prayer first, then fasting, zakat and hajj, then marriage, trade, inheritance and the courts.

usul-al-fiqh.s: The science of how rulings are derived: which sources count, and how they are read.
usul-al-fiqh.l: Literally the roots of fiqh. Where fiqh gives you the answer, usul al-fiqh gives you the method: the four sources agreed by the Sunni schools are the Qur'an, the Sunnah, ijma' and qiyas, together with rules for language, abrogation and conflicting evidence. Al-Shafi'i's Risalah is the earliest surviving book devoted to the subject.

shariah.s: The whole of what God revealed as guidance: belief, worship, character and law together.
shariah.l: The word literally means the path to water, and the Qur'an uses it for the way God set out for the Prophet to follow. It is far wider than law in the modern sense; most of it concerns prayer, fasting, honesty and family, and only a small portion concerns courts and punishment. Shari'ah is the revelation itself, while fiqh is the scholarly understanding of it, and collapsing the two makes human opinion sound divine.

ijtihad.s: The disciplined effort of a qualified scholar to derive a ruling from the sources.
ijtihad.l: The root means to exert oneself to the limit. It applies where the texts are not decisive, since nobody performs ijtihad against a clear and settled ruling. Classical scholars set demanding conditions for the mujtahid, including Arabic, command of the Qur'an and hadith, and knowledge of where consensus lies. The Prophet taught that one who judges by ijtihad and is right has two rewards, and one who tries sincerely and is wrong still has one.

taqlid.s: Following a qualified scholar's ruling without knowing the underlying evidence yourself.
taqlid.l: It is what most Muslims do most of the time, and the Qur'an tells those who do not know to ask those who do. Scholars differ over its limits: some hold a layperson should commit to one school for coherence, others allow asking any trustworthy scholar, and all agree taqlid is not followed against a clear text one actually knows. The word is also used critically, for copying without thought, which is a different matter from consulting an expert.

madhhab.s: A school of law: a settled method of deriving rulings, carried by generations of scholars.
madhhab.l: The plural is madhahib, and the word means a way gone along. Four Sunni schools survive with a living scholarly tradition: Hanafi, Maliki, Shafi'i and Hanbali. They agree on the pillars and on the great majority of rulings, and differ mostly in method and in detail. A madhhab is not a sect, and a Hanafi and a Shafi'i pray behind one another without difficulty.

hanafi.s: The school of Abu Hanifah, the most widely followed, known for careful reasoning and analogy.
hanafi.l: Named for Abu Hanifah al-Nu'man ibn Thabit of Kufa, who died in 150 AH, and set down by his students Abu Yusuf and al-Shaybani. It is the school of most Muslims in Turkey, the Balkans, Central Asia, South Asia and much of the Levant and Egypt. Its distinctive features include a strong use of istihsan and of local custom, and a separate ruling category of wajib standing just below fard.

maliki.s: The school of Malik ibn Anas of Madinah, weighted towards the practice of that city.
maliki.l: Malik died in 179 AH, and his Muwatta is among the earliest surviving books of hadith and law together. The school prevails across North and West Africa and parts of the Gulf. It gives particular weight to 'amal ahl al-Madinah, the living practice of the people of Madinah, on the reasoning that a whole city's inherited habit is itself evidence, and it makes heavy use of maslahah and of blocking the means.

shafii.s: The school of al-Shafi'i, known for tight textual method and a systematic theory of sources.
shafii.l: Muhammad ibn Idris al-Shafi'i died in 204 AH and wrote the Risalah, the first surviving work of usul al-fiqh. His school prevails in Egypt, East Africa, Yemen, Kurdistan and much of Southeast Asia. It leans on hadith more readily than the Hanafis do, and it rejects istihsan as a source in its own right, holding that preference without evidence is lawmaking.

hanbali.s: The school of Ahmad ibn Hanbal, the most text bound of the four, strongest in Arabia.
hanbali.l: Ahmad ibn Hanbal died in 241 AH and is remembered as much for his endurance under persecution as for his law. In worship the school stays close to the reports and is cautious about opinion. In transactions it is unusually permissive, holding that any contract is valid unless something forbids it. Ibn Taymiyyah and Ibn al-Qayyim wrote from within this school.

ijma.s: The agreement of the qualified scholars of one generation on a single ruling.
ijma.l: It is the third of the four agreed sources, after the Qur'an and the Sunnah. Certain ijma' is rare, and mostly concerns matters everyone already knows, such as the five daily prayers and the prohibition of wine. Scholars differ over whether a consensus after the Companions can ever be verified across a scattered world, so a claim of ijma' is something to check rather than accept on sight.

qiyas.s: Analogy: extending a known ruling to a new case that shares the same underlying reason.
qiyas.l: The classic example is extending the prohibition of wine to every intoxicant, because the reason behind the ruling is intoxication rather than grapes. It has four parts: the original case, the new case, the ruling, and the 'illah or effective cause, and identifying the 'illah is the difficult part. All four Sunni schools accept qiyas as a source; the Zahiri school rejected it and worked from the texts alone.

urf.s: Local custom, which fiqh accepts as a decider where revelation has left a matter open.
urf.l: If a contract says a reasonable quantity, or a delivery in good time, it is 'urf that decides what those words mean. It cannot make lawful what the texts forbid; it fills gaps and defines undefined terms. Because customs change, rulings resting on 'urf change with them, which is why the same school can give different answers in different centuries or countries without contradicting itself.

maslahah.s: Public benefit, weighed as a legal consideration where no specific text settles the matter.
maslahah.l: Its full name is al-maslahah al-mursalah, the untethered benefit, meaning one that revelation neither commands nor forbids by name. Registering marriages, compiling the Qur'an into one volume and building prisons were all defended this way. The schools differ over how far it may reach: Malikis and Hanbalis use it most freely, Shafi'is more narrowly, and all of them insist it can never overturn a clear text.

darurah.s: Necessity: the state in which something forbidden becomes permitted in order to preserve life.
darurah.l: The Qur'an allows a starving person to eat forbidden meat without sin, provided he is not seeking to transgress. Jurists built a maxim on it, that necessity makes the forbidden permitted, and bounded it with a second, that necessity is measured strictly by its extent. Hardship and inconvenience are not darurah; the classical threshold is real danger to life, limb, mind, lineage or property.

rukhsah.s: A concession: permission to do the easier thing when a recognised excuse applies.
rukhsah.l: Shortening prayer while travelling, breaking the fast when ill, and wiping over socks are all rukhsah. The Qur'an states plainly that God intends ease for you and does not intend hardship, and the Prophet is reported to have said God loves His concessions to be taken as He loves His commands to be obeyed. Taking a concession you genuinely qualify for is not weakness, and refusing one out of scruple is not extra piety.

azimah.s: The original ruling, before any concession applies: the default rather than the exception.
azimah.l: 'Azimah and rukhsah are a matched pair. Praying four rak'ahs is the 'azimah; shortening them on a journey is the rukhsah. Scholars differ over which is better for someone who qualifies for a concession, though most hold that where the Prophet clearly took the concession himself, as with breaking the fast on a hard journey, taking it is preferred.

halal.s: Permitted. Anything revelation has not forbidden, which is the great majority of things.
halal.l: The word means loosed or untied. In ordinary worldly matters the default is permission, so the burden of proof lies on whoever claims a thing is forbidden, not on the person doing it. In food it usually means meat slaughtered properly and free of pork, blood and intoxicants. But halal covers earnings, speech and work at least as much as it covers dinner.

haram.s: Forbidden. Leaving it is rewarded, and doing it deliberately is a sin.
haram.l: The list is far shorter than people assume: shirk, killing, theft, interest, intoxicants, pork, gambling, zina, and injustice to others. Something is haram only on clear evidence, and calling a disputed matter haram is itself a serious step, since the Qur'an warns against declaring things lawful and unlawful without knowledge. The same root also means sacred and inviolable, which is why the mosque in Makkah is al-Masjid al-Haram.

makruh.s: Disliked but not forbidden: leaving it is rewarded, doing it brings no sin.
makruh.l: Wasting water in wudu, and eating raw garlic before going to the mosque, are standard examples. Hanafis split the category in two: makruh tahriman, close to forbidden and sinful to do, and makruh tanzihan, merely unbecoming. The other three schools work with a single category. So a Hanafi and a Shafi'i can use the same word and mean noticeably different things, which is worth checking before you take offence or comfort.

mustahabb.s: Recommended: rewarded if done, with no blame for leaving it.
mustahabb.l: It covers the great mass of good practice, from the voluntary prayers around the obligatory ones to greeting people first and using the siwak. Mustahabb, mandub, sunnah and nafl are used almost interchangeably, with fine distinctions between the schools. Nobody is called to account for missing a mustahabb, which is why it should never be pressed on another person as though it were fard.

mandub.s: The technical term in legal theory for a recommended act: the same idea as mustahabb.
mandub.l: Literally, something invited or called to. Legal theorists prefer mandub, while practical books of fiqh usually say mustahabb or simply sunnah. Hanafis grade the recommended further, into sunnah mu'akkadah, which the Prophet kept up consistently, and mustahabb or nafl, which he did from time to time. On that grading, habitually dropping a sunnah mu'akkadah is blameworthy, though it is not sin in the way abandoning a fard is.

mubah.s: Neutral: neither rewarded nor blamed, permitted and left entirely to your choice.
mubah.l: Which colour you wear and what you eat for breakfast are mubah, and most of ordinary life sits inside this category. A mubah act can become worship through intention, since eating so as to have strength to pray is rewarded, and sleeping so as to rise for fajr is rewarded. This is where the maxim that matters are judged by their intentions does its quietest and most useful work.

fard.s: Obligatory: required by decisive evidence, and sinful to abandon without an excuse.
fard.l: The five daily prayers, the fast of Ramadan and zakat are fard. Hanafis reserve the word for what is proved beyond doubt and use wajib for what rests on a single strong report, so for them denying a fard is disbelief while denying a wajib is not. The other three schools treat fard and wajib as two names for one thing, which explains a good deal of apparent disagreement in books.

wajib.s: Obligatory. In the Hanafi school, a step below fard, resting on slightly weaker evidence.
wajib.l: For Malikis, Shafi'is and Hanbalis, wajib and fard are two words for one category. Hanafis separate them: the witr prayer and the sacrifice at Eid al-Adha are wajib rather than fard, so neglecting them is sinful while denying them is not disbelief. In hajj the distinction has a practical edge, since a missed wajib can be repaired by a sacrifice while a missed pillar cannot.

fard-ayn.s: An individual obligation: every responsible Muslim must perform it personally.
fard-ayn.l: Prayer, fasting Ramadan, zakat when you own the nisab, and hajj once if you are able. Nobody can discharge these on your behalf, and another person doing them does not lift them from you. Learning enough to practise your own religion is also fard 'ayn, which is why the basics of purification, prayer and honest earning are everybody's business and not only the scholars'.

fard-kifayah.s: A communal obligation: if enough people carry it out, it is lifted from everyone else.
fard-kifayah.l: The funeral prayer, memorising the Qur'an, medicine, and returning a greeting given to a group all fall here. If nobody does it, everyone capable shares the blame; once it is covered, it becomes merely recommended for the rest. Much of what a community actually needs, from judges and doctors to those who wash the dead, is organised under this single heading.

niyyah-fiqh.s: Intention, which decides what an act legally is, not merely whether it is rewarded.
niyyah-fiqh.l: The Prophet said that actions are only by their intentions, and jurists turned this into the first of the great legal maxims: matters are judged by their objectives. It settles whether a wash is a bath or a wudu, whether money handed over is a gift, a loan or a repayment, and whether ambiguous words of divorce take effect. In worship the intention lives in the heart; in contracts what you say and do binds you as well, because other people have relied on it.

nikah.s: The Islamic marriage contract, formed by offer, acceptance, witnesses and a mahr.
nikah.l: The word means to join. Marriage in Islam is a contract rather than a sacrament, and consent is its foundation: the Prophet annulled a marriage a woman told him she had not agreed to. Requirements differ a little between schools: the majority require a wali to contract on the bride's behalf, while Hanafis allow an adult woman to contract her own. Marriage is strongly encouraged rather than obligatory, and celibacy as a religious discipline has no place in Islam.

mahr.s: The gift of money or property the groom owes the bride, which belongs to her alone.
mahr.l: The Qur'an tells men to give it graciously, as a free gift. It is not a bride price paid to her family, and nobody else has any claim on it. It may be paid at once or deferred, and there is no fixed amount: the Prophet told one man to look for even an iron ring, and in the end married him to her for the Qur'an he had memorised, while extravagance was discouraged. If a marriage ends before consummation, half is normally due.

walimah.s: The wedding feast held after the marriage, and a strongly confirmed sunnah on the groom.
walimah.l: The Prophet told 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf to hold one even if only with a single sheep, and he taught that answering the invitation is a duty on those invited unless they have an excuse. Most scholars hold the walimah itself is a confirmed sunnah rather than obligatory. He also warned against a feast to which only the rich are invited and the poor are turned away, which is the part most often forgotten.

talaq.s: Divorce pronounced by the husband, which Islamic law permits but treats as a last resort.
talaq.l: The Qur'an gives it a whole surah and sets out a careful procedure: a single pronouncement, then a waiting period during which the couple may simply resume, with two further chances before the separation becomes final. Three pronouncements in one sitting are counted as three by the majority and as one by a minority, and this is among the oldest live disputes in fiqh. A woman who wishes to end a marriage uses khul' or asks a judge for faskh instead.

iddah.s: The waiting period a woman observes after divorce or a husband's death before remarrying.
iddah.l: After divorce it is three quru', which Hanafis and Hanbalis read as menstrual cycles and Malikis and Shafi'is as the purities between them, or three months for a woman who does not menstruate; after a husband's death, four months and ten days; and if she is pregnant, until she gives birth. Its purposes are to show there is no pregnancy, to leave room for reconciliation, and to mark the ending. In a revocable divorce she keeps housing and maintenance, and the husband may take her back without a new contract.

khul.s: Divorce sought by the wife, usually by returning the mahr in exchange for her release.
khul.l: Its basis is the Qur'anic statement that there is no blame on either of them in what she gives to be free, and the case of the wife of Thabit ibn Qays, who returned the garden he had given her. Scholars differ over whether the husband must agree or a judge may impose it, and over whether khul' counts as an irrevocable divorce or as an annulment, which changes the waiting period that follows. She does not need to prove wrongdoing to ask for it.

mahram.s: A relative you may never marry, and before whom the rules of covering are relaxed.
mahram.l: The Qur'an lists them: parents, children, siblings, aunts and uncles, nieces and nephews, along with relations formed by marriage such as a mother in law, and milk relations formed by nursing in infancy. The familiar phrase about travelling with a mahram refers to this same category, together with the husband. A cousin is not a mahram, which surprises many people, and neither is a brother in law.

awrah.s: The part of the body that must be covered, which varies by person and by setting.
awrah.l: For a man all four schools say from the navel to the knee. For a woman before unrelated men the schools differ: the majority cover everything except the face and hands, some Hanbalis and later Shafi'is include the face, and Hanafis also exempt the feet. Among other women and before mahrams the requirement is much lighter, and in prayer it differs again. It is a rule about dignity in company, not a claim that the body is shameful.

hijab.s: The covering a Muslim woman wears in public, most often a headscarf with modest clothing.
hijab.l: The command to draw the khimar over the neckline stands in Surah al-Nur, directly after the command to believing men to lower their gaze; the outer garment, the jilbab, is in Surah al-Ahzab. The word itself means a screen or curtain, and in the Qur'an it usually means a barrier rather than a garment; the everyday sense of headscarf is later usage. The schools agree on covering the hair and body and differ over the face and hands.

riba.s: Interest or unjust increase on a loan or exchange, forbidden in the Qur'an in severe terms.
riba.l: Two forms are named: riba al-fadl, an unequal swap of the same commodity hand to hand, and riba al-nasi'ah, the increase charged for time, which is what an interest bearing loan involves. The Qur'an permits trade and forbids riba in the same breath, and the objection is to money multiplying from money with no shared risk and no real goods. Scholars differ sharply over how far the ruling extends into modern banking, and Islamic finance is the attempt to answer that.

gharar.s: Excessive uncertainty in a contract, which makes the deal invalid.
gharar.l: The Prophet forbade the gharar sale, and the stock examples jurists give are the young of an animal not yet born, and the fish still in the water. The problem is not risk, which every honest trade carries, but not knowing what you are buying, at what price, or whether it exists at all. Minor uncertainty is tolerated, since no contract is perfectly precise. Scholars invoke gharar when questioning conventional insurance and some derivative contracts, and takaful was designed as an answer to it.

aqd.s: A contract: a binding agreement formed by an offer and its acceptance.
aqd.l: The word means a knot or a tie, and Surah al-Ma'idah opens by telling believers to fulfil their contracts. Fiqh requires clear terms, a lawful subject matter, and consent free of coercion and deception. The Hanbali rule is the most generous of the four, holding any contract valid unless a text forbids it, which leaves wide room for new commercial forms, and modern Islamic finance leans on that opening.

amanah.s: A trust: anything placed in your care that you must return, or use exactly as agreed.
amanah.l: The Qur'an commands rendering trusts back to those they belong to. Legally, someone holding an amanah is not liable for loss that occurs without negligence, which is what separates a deposit from a loan or from property seized. The word is also used morally, for the trust of life, of knowledge and of public office, and its opposite is khiyanah, betrayal, which the Prophet named among the signs of hypocrisy.

waqf-endowment.s: A permanent charitable endowment: property held forever so that its income keeps serving a purpose.
waqf-endowment.l: 'Umar asked the Prophet about land he had acquired at Khaybar and was told to hold the property itself and give away its produce, which became the model. Once made, a waqf cannot be sold, given away or inherited, and it is administered for its stated beneficiaries, whether a mosque, a school, a well or a family. Historically waqf funded most of the Muslim world's hospitals, libraries and colleges, and it remains the fullest form of ongoing charity.

wasiyyah.s: A bequest: instructions for up to a third of your estate, taking effect after death.
wasiyyah.l: The Qur'an mentions it before the inheritance shares, and debts are settled before both. Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas asked about leaving his whole estate to charity and was told a third, and that even a third is a great deal. A wasiyyah cannot be made in favour of someone who already inherits, since their share is fixed by revelation, so it is used for non heirs, for charity, and for burial and guardianship instructions.

mirath.s: Islamic inheritance: fixed shares of an estate distributed among relatives named in the Qur'an.
mirath.l: It is also called 'ilm al-fara'id, the science of the fixed portions, and it is the most mathematical corner of fiqh. The order is debts first, then any bequest up to a third, then the shares. Some heirs take a stated fraction while the remainder passes to the nearest male agnate, and because the cases interlock, one heir's presence can change another's share entirely. Most families need someone who knows the subject to work an estate out correctly.

qisas.s: Equal retaliation for murder or injury, which the victim's family may always waive for compensation.
qisas.l: The Qur'an calls it life for you, meaning that a known and strictly limited penalty restrains the endless blood feuds it replaced. It requires a court, proof and deliberate intent, and it is never a private act of revenge. The Qur'an then urges pardon and calls forgiving it an expiation for the one who forgives, and the family may accept diyah or waive everything, which classical practice treated as the better road.

diyah.s: Blood money: compensation paid to a victim's family for a killing or an injury.
diyah.l: The Qur'an prescribes it for accidental killing, alongside the freeing of a slave, and it is also what a family receives when they waive qisas for a deliberate one. The classical measure is one hundred camels, which jurists converted into gold, silver or currency, with fixed fractions for the loss of an eye, a hand or a tooth. In the classical rules the payment falls on the killer's kin group, the 'aqilah, an early form of shared insurance.

hudud.s: The small set of fixed penalties named in revelation, hedged about with very strict proof.
hudud.l: The singular is hadd, a limit; the name comes from the Qur'an's phrase the limits of God, which it uses more widely. Jurists usually count between four and seven: theft, zina, false accusation of zina, highway robbery, and for most, drinking wine and apostasy. The evidence required is deliberately near impossible, four upright eyewitnesses to the act itself in zina, and a settled maxim holds that hudud are averted by any doubt. Confessions may be withdrawn, and the classical record shows these penalties were rarely carried out.

tazir.s: Discretionary punishment, set by a judge for offences that carry no fixed penalty.
tazir.l: The word means correction. It covers the vast majority of wrongdoing, from fraud and bribery to public nuisance, and it can be a warning, a fine, imprisonment or public rebuke. The judge weighs the person, the offence and the circumstances, and most jurists hold that ta'zir must stay below the level of a hadd. This flexible category, and not the hudud, is where classical Islamic criminal justice actually did its daily work.

bayah.s: A pledge of allegiance, given to a ruler, or in Sufi orders to a spiritual guide.
bayah.l: The word comes from bay', a sale, since the one who pledges gives loyalty and receives protection in return. The Qur'an records the pledge under the tree and the pledge of the believing women, and the Prophet took bay'ah on obedience in what is good, a condition scholars stress: there is no obedience to a creature in disobedience to the Creator. In Sufi orders bay'ah to a shaykh is a commitment to a path of training, which is a different use of the same word.

dhimmah.s: The historic covenant under which non Muslims in a Muslim state kept their religion and protection.
dhimmah.l: The word means liability or covenant, and ahl al-dhimmah are the people it covered. In exchange for jizyah they were exempt from military service and from zakat, kept their own courts in matters of personal law, and had their lives, property and places of worship protected; the Prophet warned that whoever wrongs a covenanted person will find the Prophet himself his opponent on the Day of Judgement. It was a premodern arrangement of defined but unequal status, and most contemporary scholars treat it as superseded by common citizenship.

jizyah.s: A tax historically paid by non Muslim men under Muslim rule, in place of military service.
jizyah.l: It is named once in the Qur'an. Classical law exempted women, children, the elderly, the poor, the disabled and monks, and the rate was scaled to ability to pay. 'Umar ibn al-Khattab is reported to have granted a pension from the treasury to an elderly Jewish beggar rather than take jizyah from him. Muslims meanwhile paid zakat and were liable for military service, so the comparison was never one tax against none.

zakat-al-mal.s: Zakat on wealth: normally one fortieth of qualifying savings held for a full lunar year.
zakat-al-mal.l: It is distinguished from zakat al-fitr, the small fixed measure of food given per person at the end of Ramadan. It falls due on cash, gold, silver, trade stock and recoverable debts once they pass the nisab and a lunar year has turned, while crops, livestock and mined wealth have their own rates and no year requirement. Your home, personal belongings and the tools of your trade are exempt. Scholars differ over pensions, shares, and gold jewellery in regular use.

fatwa.s: A scholar's answer to a specific question: advice, not a court judgement.
fatwa.l: The one who gives it is a mufti and the one who asks is a mustafti. A fatwa compels nobody, it can differ from another qualified scholar's fatwa without either being wrong, and a good one depends closely on the asker's circumstances, which is why lifting someone else's fatwa off the internet can mislead you badly. A judge's ruling is the opposite: binding, and it settles the case for everyone in it.

qadi.s: A judge in an Islamic court, whose ruling binds, unlike a mufti's opinion.
qadi.l: Appointment as a qadi was treated as a heavy burden rather than an honour, and several of the great imams refused it outright. The office asks for knowledge, integrity and independence, and classical manuals warn a judge not to rule while angry, hungry or distracted. The instruction reported from the Prophet, not to decide between two people until you have heard from both, is quoted in nearly every book on the subject.

maqasid-al-shariah.s: The higher aims of Islamic law: what its rulings exist in order to protect.
maqasid-al-shariah.l: Al-Ghazali and later al-Shatibi set out five: religion, life, intellect, lineage and property, with dignity and sometimes freedom added by later scholars. Interests are ranked as necessities, needs and refinements, so what preserves life outweighs what merely makes life more comfortable. Maqasid explain why a ruling exists and help reasoning where the texts are silent, but most scholars insist they cannot be used to set a clear text aside.

qawaid-fiqhiyyah.s: Legal maxims: short principles that gather the pattern behind thousands of separate rulings.
qawaid-fiqhiyyah.l: Five are counted as the great ones: matters are judged by their intentions; certainty is not lifted by doubt; hardship brings ease; harm is to be removed; and custom decides. They are teaching tools and aids to reasoning rather than sources in their own right, and every one of them has recognised exceptions. Al-Suyuti's al-Ashbah wa al-Naza'ir is the best known collection.

istihsan.s: Juristic preference: setting aside a strict analogy for a stronger reason of fairness or need.
istihsan.l: It is chiefly a Hanafi and Maliki tool, used where the obvious qiyas would cause real hardship or would collide with a text, a consensus or plain necessity. The Hanafi allowance of manufacturing contracts, where the goods do not yet exist, is a standard example. Al-Shafi'i attacked istihsan in famous words, saying whoever practises it has made law himself, though his objection was to arbitrary preference rather than to reasoned exception.

istishab.s: Presumption of continuity: what was established stays in force until there is proof it changed.
istishab.l: It is why you are still in wudu when you merely doubt whether you broke it, why a missing person is presumed alive until evidence says otherwise, and why an accused person is treated as innocent until guilt is proved. It works hand in hand with the maxim that certainty is not lifted by doubt. Shafi'is and Hanbalis use it broadly, while Hanafis accept it to defend an existing state but not to establish a new right.

sadd-al-dharai.s: Blocking the means: forbidding something lawful because it reliably leads to something forbidden.
sadd-al-dharai.l: The classic proof is the Qur'anic instruction not to insult what others call upon besides God, lest they insult God in return out of ignorance. Malikis and Hanbalis use the principle heavily, while Shafi'is and Hanafis apply it more sparingly, since without limits it can be stretched to forbid nearly anything. Its mirror image, opening the means, is used to encourage whatever leads to a required good.

ikhtilaf.s: Scholarly disagreement, which classical Islam treated as normal rather than as a crisis.
ikhtilaf.l: It arises from the wording of texts, the strength of reports, differing methods, and different local customs. Scholars distinguished tolerated disagreement, where each side holds real evidence, from disagreement over what is definitively known, which is not tolerated. The Companions themselves differed and still prayed behind one another, and the standard etiquette is to act on the view you follow without condemning someone who follows another qualified one.

mukallaf.s: A person legally responsible: sane, and past the age of puberty.
mukallaf.l: The obligations of fiqh apply once both conditions are met, and the Prophet said the pen is lifted from three: the sleeper until he wakes, the child until he matures, and the one who has lost his mind until he recovers. Children are taught to pray at seven and firmly encouraged at ten, but what they do counts as voluntary and earns them reward without obligation. Puberty is judged by physical signs, or where none appear, by an age the schools commonly set around fifteen.

wali-nikah.s: The male relative who contracts a woman's marriage on her behalf, usually her father.
wali-nikah.l: Malikis, Shafi'is and Hanbalis hold a marriage invalid without one, citing the report that there is no marriage without a wali. Hanafis hold that an adult woman may contract her own marriage, though her guardian may object to a plainly unsuitable match. Whether a father may marry off a virgin daughter without her word is the oldest dispute here: Hanafis say no, the other three allowed it under conditions, Ibn Taymiyyah rejected it. The Prophet annulled the marriage of a woman whose father had contracted it against her will.

nafaqah.s: Maintenance: the husband's duty to provide housing, food and clothing for wife and children.
nafaqah.l: The Qur'an sets the measure by means, telling a man of wealth to spend from his wealth and one whose provision is straitened to spend from what God has given him. It is owed regardless of the wife's own income, since whatever she owns or earns remains hers alone. It continues through the waiting period after a revocable divorce, and a father's duty to maintain his children does not end when the marriage does.

radaah.s: Milk kinship: breastfeeding in infancy creates the same marriage bars that birth creates.
radaah.l: The Qur'an names milk mothers and milk sisters among those a man may not marry, and the Prophet said that nursing forbids what birth forbids. The schools differ over how much is enough: Shafi'is and Hanbalis require five separate feeds, while Hanafis and Malikis count any amount that reaches the stomach. All agree it must fall within the nursing years, which the majority place in the first two.

faskh.s: Annulment: a judge dissolving a marriage for a defect or a failure of duty.
faskh.l: Grounds recognised across the schools include serious undisclosed illness, impotence, insanity, desertion, imprisonment, failure to maintain, and harm. Malikis are the broadest here, allowing dissolution for harm in general, which is why courts in many countries follow them on this point even where another school prevails. Faskh differs from talaq because it uses up none of the husband's pronouncements, and from khul' because it requires no payment from the wife.

mutah.s: Temporary marriage for a fixed term, permitted in Twelver Shia law and prohibited in Sunni law.
mutah.l: Sunni scholars hold it was allowed early in Islam and then abolished by the Prophet, with reports placing the final prohibition at Khaybar or at the conquest of Makkah, and 'Umar's public ban is widely cited alongside them. Twelver Shia jurists hold the permission was never abrogated, and regulate mut'ah as a contract with a stated term and a stated dower. The same word has an unrelated sense in Sunni fiqh: a consolation payment made to a divorced wife.

zina.s: Sexual intercourse outside marriage: a major sin, and one of the fixed penalty offences.
zina.l: The Qur'an says do not go near it, calling it an immorality and an evil way, and the wording is read as forbidding the approaches to it as well as the act. The penalty carries a bar of proof so high it is almost never reached, four upright witnesses to the act itself, and the same passage punishes those who make the accusation without them. Islamic law discourages prying, and consistently prefers concealment and repentance to exposure.

riddah.s: Apostasy: abandoning Islam after having accepted it.
riddah.l: Classical law treated open apostasy as a capital offence, drawing on prophetic reports rather than on the Qur'an, which mentions apostasy several times without prescribing any worldly penalty and states plainly that there is no compulsion in religion. Hanafis did not apply the death penalty to a woman who apostatised, and jurists across the schools required that repentance be invited first. Many contemporary scholars read the classical rulings as addressing public treason within a specific political order rather than private belief, and the question is actively debated.

bay.s: Sale: the exchange of property for property by mutual consent.
bay.l: The Qur'an states that God has permitted trade and forbidden riba, and the Prophet himself worked as a merchant before prophethood. A valid sale needs a known price, a known item the seller can actually deliver, ownership or authority to sell it, and consent untouched by deception. Fiqh names many specific forms, among them salam, paid now and delivered later, and murabahah, sold at a disclosed markup.

ijarah.s: Hire or lease: paying for the use of something, or for another person's labour.
ijarah.l: The Qur'an mentions hiring a worker in the story of Musa in Madyan and instructs that a nursing mother be paid her due. The contract needs a defined benefit, a defined period and a known wage agreed in advance. The reported instruction to give the worker his wage before his sweat dries is the most quoted line in the whole chapter. In Islamic finance, ijarah is the leasing structure used in place of an interest bearing loan.

murabahah.s: A sale at a disclosed cost plus markup, widely used in Islamic banking in place of lending.
murabahah.l: In its classical form the seller states what the goods cost him and what profit he is adding, so the buyer knows both figures. Modern banks use it to finance purchases: the bank buys the asset, then sells it on to the customer at a higher price payable in instalments.
