Supporters point out that the bank takes real ownership and real risk in between; critics answer that the outcome tracks interest too closely, and the disagreement among scholars is genuine and unsettled.

mudarabah.s: A partnership where one side provides capital and the other the work, sharing agreed profits.
mudarabah.l: Losses of money fall on the investor while the working partner loses his effort, unless he was negligent or broke the terms. Profit must be divided by a stated ratio and never as a fixed sum, since a guaranteed return would quietly turn the arrangement into an interest bearing loan. Musharakah is its sibling, in which both sides put in capital and share profit and loss by agreement. Both predate Islam and were confirmed rather than invented by it, and both underpin profit sharing accounts today.

takaful.s: Cooperative insurance, built on mutual donation, offered as an alternative to conventional policies.
takaful.l: Participants contribute to a shared fund on the basis of tabarru', donation, and the fund pays claims, while an operator manages it for a fee or an agreed share. It was designed to answer the objections scholars raise against conventional insurance, namely gharar, resemblance to gambling, and interest bearing reserves. Not every scholar accepts that the difference is substantive, and some hold conventional insurance permissible under necessity where no alternative is available.

dhabihah.s: Meat from an animal slaughtered in the Islamic way, with the name of God pronounced over it.
dhabihah.l: The throat is cut swiftly with a sharp blade, severing the windpipe and the blood vessels, and the animal must be alive and treated gently beforehand; the Prophet ordered the blade to be sharpened, the animal spared distress, and the knife kept out of its sight. The Qur'an also permits the food of the People of the Book, and scholars differ over whether ordinary commercial meat in Jewish and Christian countries falls under that permission. Pork, blood, carrion and anything dedicated to other than God remain forbidden either way.

khamr.s: Intoxicants. Wine and anything else that clouds the mind, forbidden in the Qur'an.
khamr.l: The prohibition arrived in stages, ending with the command to shun it as a defilement from the work of Satan. The Prophet's rule that whatever intoxicates in large amounts is forbidden in small amounts extends the ban to every intoxicant, and it is the textbook example of qiyas at work. Hanafis kept the word khamr technically for grape wine while forbidding other intoxicants under a separate heading, arriving at the same practical result. Scholars differ over intoxicating substances used as medicine where no alternative exists.

ulum-al-hadith.s: The science of testing reports about the Prophet, deciding which are sound and which are not.
ulum-al-hadith.l: Every report is judged from two sides: the chain of people who passed it on, and the wording they carried. The classic handbook is the Muqaddimah of Ibn al-Salah, and Ibn Hajar's short Nukhbat al-Fikar is the summary students still memorise.

hadith.s: A report of what the Prophet Muhammad said, did, or quietly approved, passed down through named narrators.
hadith.l: The word means speech, or something newly told. A hadith has two parts: the chain of people who carried it, and the text they carried. A hadith is a report about the Sunnah, so a weak hadith does not become Sunnah by being printed in a book.

hadith-qudsi.s: A hadith in which the Prophet reports words from Allah that are not part of the Qur'an.
hadith-qudsi.l: The usual account is that the meaning is from Allah and the wording from the Prophet, while the Qur'an is both meaning and wording from Allah. A hadith qudsi is not recited in prayer and carries no claim of inimitability. It is also not automatically authentic; like any hadith it can be sahih, hasan or weak.

athar.s: A report from a Companion or a follower rather than from the Prophet himself.
athar.l: The word means a trace or a footprint, what is left behind after someone passes. Most scholars use athar for what stops at a Companion or a Tabi'i, and hadith for what reaches the Prophet, though some early scholars used athar for any report at all. Athar matters because Companion practice often shows what a hadith meant in the room where it was said.

khabar.s: A report; scholars use the word either as a synonym for hadith or for reports not reaching the Prophet.
khabar.l: Three usages are recorded. Some treat khabar and hadith as the same thing. Some treat khabar as the wider word, covering reports from the Prophet and from anyone else. Some reserve hadith for the Prophet and khabar for everyone else, which is why early historians were called akhbariyyun.

isnad.s: The chain of narrators who carried a hadith, listed name by name back to its source.
isnad.l: A hadith is quoted like this: so and so told me, from so and so, from so and so, that the Prophet said. Abdullah ibn al-Mubarak said the isnad is part of the religion, and that without it anyone could say whatever he wished. Few traditions built a citation system this early, or held to it this stubbornly.

sanad.s: The chain itself, the line of narrators supporting a text, used almost interchangeably with isnad.
sanad.l: The root means to lean something against a support. Strictly, sanad is the chain and isnad is the act of citing it, but in practice scholars use each word for the other. A strong sanad does not by itself make a strong hadith, because the text can still carry a hidden defect.

matn.s: The actual wording of a hadith, the part that comes after the chain of narrators.
matn.l: The word means the firm surface of the ground, or the back of something. Scholars weigh the matn as well as the chain. A text that contradicts the Qur'an, or a plain fact, or promises an enormous reward for a tiny act, is treated with suspicion even when the chain looks tidy.

rawi.s: A narrator: one of the people in the chain who heard a report and passed it on.
rawi.l: Every rawi in a chain has a file. Scholars recorded when he was born, who he studied with, how good his memory was, whether he was honest, and whether he lived long enough to have met the man he quotes. A hadith is only as strong as the weakest rawi in its chain.

riwayah.s: The act of transmitting a report, and the version transmitted; its partner science is dirayah, understanding it.
riwayah.l: Ilm al-riwayah is the work of carrying reports accurately. Ilm al-dirayah is the work of judging and understanding them. A person can be excellent at one and poor at the other, which is why some famous narrators were not jurists and some great jurists narrated little.

muhaddith.s: A scholar of hadith who has studied the chains, the narrators and the defects, not merely read collections.
muhaddith.l: The ranks are informal but real. A talib is a student, a muhaddith works in the field, a hafiz has mastered a great number of chains, and titles like hujjah were given to a handful of men. Knowing many hadiths is not the same as being a muhaddith; the skill lies in judging them.

hafiz.s: In hadith, a master who has memorised a very large number of reports together with their chains.
hafiz.l: In everyday speech today hafiz means someone who has memorised the Qur'an, and that use is fine. In hadith books it is a technical rank above muhaddith, given to men like Ibn Hajar al-Asqalani, who is often called simply al-Hafiz. The word means one who guards something.

ilm-al-rijal.s: The biographical science of the narrators: who they were, whom they met, and how reliable each was.
ilm-al-rijal.l: Tens of thousands of narrators were catalogued by generation, or tabaqat, so a claimed meeting between two men could be checked against their lifespans. The large references include al-Bukhari's al-Tarikh al-Kabir, Ibn Abi Hatim's al-Jarh wa al-Ta'dil, and al-Mizzi's Tahdhib al-Kamal. Ibn Hajar's Taqrib al-Tahdhib condenses the verdict on each man into a line or two.

jarh-wa-tadil.s: The discipline of criticising or vouching for narrators, so that a chain can be judged fairly.
jarh-wa-tadil.l: Jarh means to wound, ta'dil to declare upright. Scholars used a graded vocabulary, from thiqah thiqah at the top down to kadhdhab at the bottom, and applied it to teachers, friends and family without flinching. The working rule is that a criticism which explains itself outweighs a general word of praise, and that a critic known for harshness is read with that in mind. This was not backbiting; it was quality control on what people were told God's Messenger said.

thiqah.s: A trustworthy narrator: upright in character and accurate in memory, the two conditions held together.
thiqah.l: Uprightness without accuracy gives you a sincere man who misremembers. Accuracy without uprightness gives you a sharp man who lies. Only both together make a thiqah. Ranks below it include saduq, meaning truthful but slightly less precise, and layyin, meaning soft or weak.

adalah.s: The uprightness of a narrator: sane, adult, Muslim, not openly sinful, not known for shameful habits.
adalah.l: Adalah is about character, not perfection. A narrator does not need to be a saint, but he must not be known for lying, for open sin, or for behaviour suggesting he does not care what people think of him. It is one half of being thiqah. The other half is dabt.

dabt.s: The accuracy of a narrator: how well he held the report, in memory or in a guarded book.
dabt.l: Two kinds are recognised: precision of the chest, meaning memory, and precision of the book, meaning a written copy kept safely and not lent out carelessly. Light weakness here drops a hadith from sahih to hasan. Heavy weakness, where a man's errors outnumber his sound reports, drops it further.

majhul.s: An unknown narrator, whose identity or whose reliability the scholars could not establish.
majhul.l: Two kinds are distinguished. Majhul al-ayn is a man nobody names except a single student, so we do not really know who he is. Majhul al-hal, also called mastur, is a man we can identify but whose reliability nobody recorded. A chain containing either is weak, since a report is worth only what its weakest link is worth.

matruk.s: A report from a narrator the scholars abandoned, usually one accused of lying or of gross error.
matruk.l: Matruk sits just above fabricated. It is described as severely weak, da'if jiddan, and unlike ordinary weakness it cannot be repaired by supporting chains. When a book says a narrator is matruk al-hadith, the discussion is effectively over.

tadlis.s: Wording a chain so that a gap or a weak teacher is hidden, without stating an outright lie.
tadlis.l: The word comes from trading in dim light so the buyer cannot see the flaw. The classic form is a narrator saying from so and so about a man he met but did not hear this particular report from. Scholars listed the known mudallisin in ranks, and as a rule they do not accept such a narrator's report unless he says plainly that he heard it.

ananah.s: A chain that says only from so and so, without stating that the narrator actually heard the report.
ananah.l: Such a chain is accepted if the narrator is not known for tadlis and could plausibly have met his source. Al-Bukhari held that a proven meeting must be established; Muslim held that living in the same period with the possibility of meeting is enough, and argued the point in the introduction to his Sahih. The disagreement is narrow, but it changes the verdict on a good number of chains.

sama.s: Receiving a hadith by hearing it directly from a teacher, the strongest of the ways to take a report.
sama.l: Scholars listed several ways of receiving hadith, in descending strength: hearing the teacher recite it, reading it back to him, a written licence, being handed a manuscript, correspondence, and finding a book with no licence at all. The wording of a chain tells you which way was used, so haddathana means he narrated to us in person, while akhbarana usually signals that it was read back to him.

ijazah.s: A teacher's licence permitting a student to transmit a text or a collection onward.
ijazah.l: An ijazah is a link in a living chain: the holder can say he received this book from his teacher, who received it from his, back to the author. It is weaker than hearing every word in person, and scholars debated how much weight it carries on its own. It is still issued today, most often for the Qur'an and for the six books.

sahih.s: A hadith that meets all five conditions of authenticity, with nothing missing and no hidden flaw.
sahih.l: The five conditions are an unbroken chain, every narrator upright, every narrator accurate, no contradiction of stronger narrators, and no hidden defect. Sahih is a verdict about how safely the report reached us, not a claim that its wording is revealed like the Qur'an. A lower grade, sahih li-ghayrihi, is lifted to this level by supporting chains.

hasan.s: A hadith meeting every condition of sahih except that one narrator's accuracy falls slightly short.
hasan.l: Hasan means good. It is a working grade: acceptable as evidence in law, one step below sahih. Al-Tirmidhi made the term widely used, and later scholars spent great effort defining it, since the line between light weakness and real weakness is a matter of trained judgement.

daif.s: A hadith that fails one of the conditions of soundness, through a broken chain or a faulty narrator.
daif.l: Weak does not mean false. It means the report did not arrive with enough support to be relied upon. Weakness has degrees, from a slight gap that other chains can repair, up to a narrator accused of lying, which nothing can repair. Whether a weak hadith may be used to encourage good deeds is an old disagreement among scholars rather than a settled rule.

mawdu.s: A fabricated report, invented and then attached to the Prophet; not really a hadith at all.
mawdu.l: The word means placed, or set down, as in something put there by a human hand. Fabrications were made for many motives: sectarian argument, storytelling, flattery of rulers, and misplaced zeal for encouraging worship. The Prophet's warning against deliberately lying about him is among the most widely transmitted reports in existence. Scholars wrote whole books listing fabrications so people could recognise them.

la-asla-lahu.s: A verdict meaning the saying has no chain at all, so it cannot even be graded.
la-asla-lahu.l: This is stronger than calling something weak. A weak hadith has a chain that fails; a saying with no basis was never transmitted in the first place. Such sayings are usually folk wisdom, or a scholar's own phrase that drifted into quotation marks. A great deal of what circulates as hadith online belongs here.

hasan-li-ghayrihi.s: A weak hadith raised to the level of hasan because other chains carry the same meaning.
hasan-li-ghayrihi.l: This only works when the weakness is mild, such as a narrator with a poor memory, and never when a narrator is accused of lying. Two or three light chains leaning on one another can hold a report up. Scholars differ over how much support is enough, which is why the same hadith is sometimes graded hasan by one and weak by another.

sahih-li-ghayrihi.s: A hasan hadith lifted to sahih because it is reported through more than one chain.
sahih-li-ghayrihi.l: Sahih li-dhatihi is sound in itself, by a single strong chain. Sahih li-ghayrihi is sound because of what stands beside it. Both are acted upon, and books of takhrij often write only sahih without saying which of the two they mean.

hasan-sahih.s: Al-Tirmidhi's double grading, which later scholars have explained in several different ways.
hasan-sahih.l: Read literally it sounds like calling one thing good and excellent at once. The best known explanation, from Ibn Hajar, is that where the hadith has a single chain the phrase means some scholars judged it hasan and others sahih, and where it has several chains one is hasan and another sahih. Other scholars read it differently. It is safest to treat the phrase as meaning acceptable rather than as a precise grade.

hukm.s: The verdict placed on a hadith, such as sahih, hasan, weak or fabricated.
hukm.l: A hukm is the end of a piece of work, not the beginning: it summarises the state of every narrator and every link in the chain. Two careful scholars can reach different verdicts on the same report, and that is normal rather than scandalous. In fiqh the same word means a legal ruling, which is a different subject.

takhrij.s: Tracing a hadith to the books that recorded it, gathering its chains, and then grading it.
takhrij.l: The work has three steps: find where it was narrated, collect every route it came by, and weigh them together. It is the step most often skipped when a hadith is quoted online. A proper takhrij gives the source and the verdict, so a reader can check the claim instead of trusting whoever is quoting it.

mutawatir.s: A report carried at every stage by so many people that they could not all have agreed on a lie.
mutawatir.l: There is no fixed minimum number; what matters is that the crowd is wide enough and independent enough to rule out collusion. Two kinds are described: mutawatir in wording, where the same phrase comes through, and mutawatir in meaning, where many different reports converge on one point. The five daily prayers and the number of their units reach us this way, by continuous practice as much as by text, which is a stronger route than any single chain.

ahad.s: Any hadith that does not reach the level of mutawatir, however strong its single chain may be.
ahad.l: Most hadiths, including most of the two Sahihs, are ahad. Scholars agree that an authentic ahad report is acted upon in law. They differ about creed: hadith scholars and the Hanbalis generally accept authentic ahad reports in matters of belief, while many Ash'ari, Maturidi and Hanafi theologians held that such reports give strong probability rather than certainty, and so accepted them without building charges of unbelief on them.

mashhur.s: A hadith carried by three or more narrators at each stage, well known but short of mutawatir.
mashhur.l: The word simply means famous, and there is a trap in it. People also say mashhur for a saying famous on everybody's tongue, and many of those have weak chains or none at all. Fame among the public and fame in the chains are two different things.

aziz.s: A hadith which at no stage of its chain has fewer than two narrators.
aziz.l: The word here means scarce, hard to come by. Aziz sits between gharib, which has a single narrator somewhere in the chain, and mashhur, which has three or more. The category counts how many routes exist; it does not by itself say whether the hadith is sound.

gharib.s: A hadith narrated by only one person at some point in its chain.
gharib.l: Gharib means strange, or lone. It is not a criticism in itself: the famous hadith that deeds are judged by intentions is gharib at its start and sits in both Sahihs. The same word has a second and unrelated use, gharib al-hadith, meaning the study of rare and difficult words inside hadith texts.

marfu.s: A report attributed to the Prophet himself, whether or not the chain reaching him is complete.
marfu.l: Marfu' means raised. It describes where a report ends up, not how strong it is, so a marfu' hadith may be sahih or weak. It is contrasted with mawquf, which stops at a Companion, and maqtu', which stops at a follower.

mawquf.s: A report that stops at a Companion: his own statement or action, not attributed to the Prophet.
mawquf.l: Mawquf means halted. Such reports carry real weight, since the Companions watched the practice first hand. Some mawquf statements are treated as effectively marfu', for instance when a Companion speaks about something no one could know except through revelation.

maqtu.s: A statement belonging to a Tabi'i, one of the generation after the Companions, traced no further back.
maqtu.l: Maqtu' and munqati' look alike and mean different things. Maqtu' is about whose saying it is; munqati' is about a hole in the chain. Much early tafsir and early fiqh is maqtu' material, valuable for understanding but not evidence from the Prophet.

tabii.s: A Muslim of the generation after the Companions, who met a Companion but not the Prophet.
tabii.l: The plural is tabi'un or tabi'in. They form the second layer in almost every chain, and figures like Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib, al-Hasan al-Basri and Ibn Sirin belong here. Their own statements are called maqtu', and their reports about the Prophet without naming the Companion in between are called mursal.

musnad.s: Either a hadith with a connected chain reaching the Prophet, or a book arranged by narrating Companion.
musnad.l: As a grade, musnad usually means both connected and traced to the Prophet. As a book type, a musnad gathers everything narrated by each Companion under his name, which suits tracing a narrator but makes finding a topic awkward. The largest is the Musnad of Ahmad ibn Hanbal, which holds sound and weak material together and needs a critical edition to use well.

muttasil.s: A chain in which every narrator genuinely took the report from the one named before him.
muttasil.l: Also called mawsul. Connection is the first of the five conditions of soundness, and it is checked by comparing lifetimes, travels and known teachers. A chain can be perfectly connected and still weak, if one of the connected narrators is unreliable.

mursal.s: A Tabi'i quotes the Prophet directly, leaving out the Companion who actually heard it.
mursal.l: The missing man is almost always a Companion, and Companions are held to be trustworthy, which is why the schools differ here rather than simply calling it weak. Hadith specialists generally class mursal as weak. In law, the Hanafis and Malikis accept it, al-Shafi'i accepts it only when another route supports it, and reports from Ahmad show acceptance with conditions. Later scholars also separated the mursal of the senior followers, which is stronger, from that of the juniors.

munqati.s: A chain with a break in it: a narrator missing somewhere in the middle.
munqati.l: The word means cut. It is the general term for a gap that is not at the start of the chain, not at the Companion's place at the end, and not two names deep, since each of those carries its own label. Any break makes a report weak, because the missing man is unknown and could be anyone at all.

mudal.s: A chain missing two or more narrators in a row, a wider break than munqati'.
mudal.l: The word suggests something troublesome and hard to solve. It is more serious than a single missing link, since a gap that size can hide an entire generation. When a later writer quotes the Prophet with no chain at all, the result is usually mu'dal in effect.

muallaq.s: A chain with its beginning cut off, where the author omits the narrators nearest to himself.
muallaq.l: The word means hung, as though the chain dangles with nothing above it. Al-Bukhari includes many mu'allaq reports in his Sahih, and scholars read them by their wording: those he states firmly, in the active form, are generally reliable and usually connected elsewhere in the book, while those he introduces with a passive form such as it is narrated are weaker. Ibn Hajar traced their full chains in a separate work.

shadhdh.s: An acceptable narrator contradicts someone stronger, so his version is set aside as odd.
shadhdh.l: The point is not that the man is weak. It is that when a reliable narrator's version cannot stand beside the version of narrators who are more reliable or more numerous, one of the two must be a mistake. The stronger version is then called mahfuz, the preserved one. Freedom from shudhudh is one of the five conditions of a sahih hadith.

munkar.s: A weak narrator contradicts a reliable one, or reports alone something nobody else reports.
munkar.l: The opposite is called ma'ruf, the known version. Definitions varied: earlier critics sometimes used munkar simply for a lone report from a weak narrator, with no contradiction involved. Note that munkar here is a technical grade for a report, unrelated to munkar meaning a wrong act, and unrelated to the angel of that name.

illah.s: A hidden flaw in a hadith that looks sound on the surface, found only by expert comparison.
illah.l: A hadith carrying one is called mu'allal. The defects are subtle: a report actually stopped at a Companion but raised to the Prophet by one narrator, or two chains quietly merged into one. Detecting them took men who had memorised the variants of thousands of chains, and the great books on ilal, such as those of Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Daraqutni, are among the most demanding in the field.

mudraj.s: A hadith with words inserted into it, usually a narrator's explanation that later sounded like the Prophet's speech.
mudraj.l: Insertions happen in the text and, less often, in the chain. The usual sign is a phrase that explains an unfamiliar word, or that reads like a legal clause in the middle of plain speech. Scholars caught them by finding other versions where those same words appear separately as the narrator's own comment.

maqlub.s: A hadith in which something has been switched, such as two narrators' names or two halves of a sentence.
maqlub.l: The word means turned over. Sometimes the swap is an honest slip; sometimes it was deliberate, done to test a scholar's memory or to make a chain look more impressive. A well known account describes the scholars of Baghdad testing al-Bukhari with deliberately switched chains, and his returning each text to the chain it belonged to.

mudtarib.s: A hadith narrated in versions that clash, with no way to prefer one over the other.
mudtarib.l: The word describes something shaking, unsteady on its feet. If one version can be shown to be stronger, the problem disappears and the weaker is simply set aside; idtirab is declared only when the versions are of equal weight and cannot be reconciled. It is a rare verdict, and it makes the hadith weak.

mutabaah.s: A second chain supporting the first through the same Companion, showing a narrator was not alone.
mutabaah.l: If a hadith comes only through one shaky narrator, and then a second route turns up where somebody else narrates it from the same teacher, the doubt about that man's memory eases. A full mutaba'ah agrees from the narrator himself; a partial one joins the chain further up. When the support comes through a different Companion instead, it is called a shahid.

shahid.s: A supporting report of the same meaning narrated through a different Companion.
shahid.l: The word means witness. Where a mutaba'ah props up a particular narrator, a shahid props up the content itself from another direction. Several lightly weak reports with different Companions behind them can together raise a hadith to hasan li-ghayrihi, provided none of them is severely weak.

itibar.s: The search through the books for other chains of a hadith, to see whether anything supports it.
itibar.l: I'tibar is the process; mutaba'ah and shahid are what the process finds. It is the step that decides whether a weak report can be strengthened or must be left where it is. Searchable databases have made the gathering faster without making the judgement any easier.

mukhtalif-al-hadith.s: The science of handling two sound hadiths that appear to contradict one another.
mukhtalif-al-hadith.l: The order of work, as the hadith scholars and most jurists set it out, is: reconcile them if both can be true in different situations, then check whether one came later and replaced the other, then prefer the stronger if neither of those works, and finally suspend judgement. Hanafi jurists run the same steps in a different order, looking for abrogation before reconciliation. Al-Shafi'i wrote the earliest surviving book on this, and Ibn Qutaybah wrote a well known one answering critics of hadith. Most apparent contradictions dissolve once the setting of each report is known.

fadail-al-amal.s: The old question of whether a weak hadith may be used to encourage deeds already known to be good.
fadail-al-amal.l: Three positions exist. Some scholars refuse it outright, holding that nothing should be attributed to the Prophet unless it is established. The majority allow it under conditions: the weakness must be light, the deed must already rest on something authentic, and nobody should believe the Prophet actually said the words. All three agree that a weak hadith does not establish a point of belief or a ruling, though some early jurists preferred a weak report to their own reasoning when a chapter held nothing else.

riwayah-bil-mana.s: Narrating a hadith in one's own words while keeping its meaning, rather than the exact wording.
riwayah-bil-mana.l: This is why the same event appears with different phrasing in different books. The majority allowed it for someone who knows Arabic precisely and understands what the words are doing, while a strict minority insisted on the wording as heard. Certain texts were held back from it, such as the supplications the Prophet taught word for word.

kutub-sittah.s: The six hadith collections that became the standard reference set in Sunni Islam.
kutub-sittah.l: They are Sahih al-Bukhari, Sahih Muslim, Sunan Abi Dawud, Jami' al-Tirmidhi, Sunan al-Nasa'i and Sunan Ibn Majah. The list settled slowly, and some earlier scholars put Malik's Muwatta or al-Darimi's Sunan in the sixth place instead of Ibn Majah. Being in these books is not itself a grade: only the two Sahihs claim soundness throughout, while the four Sunan contain weak material their authors often flagged.

sahihayn.s: The two Sahihs, of al-Bukhari and Muslim, the most rigorously screened collections in Sunni Islam.
sahihayn.l: Both authors set out to include only what they judged authentic, and these two books were received by the community with an acceptance given to no others. A small number of their reports were criticised by later specialists such as al-Daraqutni, and most of those criticisms concern a particular chain rather than the meaning of the text. Saying a hadith is in the Sahihayn normally ends the argument about its authenticity.

muttafaq-alayh.s: Reported by both al-Bukhari and Muslim, which is the highest ordinary grade of authenticity.
muttafaq-alayh.l: The phrase means agreed upon. In most books it refers to the two of them together, narrating through the same Companion. Some authors stretch it to include the Musnad of Ahmad as well, so it is worth checking what a particular writer means by it.

sahih-al-bukhari.s: The collection of Muhammad ibn Isma'il al-Bukhari, held to be the soundest book after the Qur'an.
sahih-al-bukhari.l: Its full title describes it as a sifted, connected, authentic collection. Al-Bukhari arranged it by chapter, and his chapter headings carry his own legal conclusions, so the book argues as well as reports. He required proof that a narrator actually met the person he quotes, a stricter rule than Muslim's. Reports repeat across chapters because he cites one hadith in several places for several points, which is why the raw entry count is far larger than the number of distinct hadiths.

sahih-muslim.s: The collection of Muslim ibn al-Hajjaj, second of the two Sahihs and the better organised of them.
sahih-muslim.l: Muslim gathered all the chains of a hadith in one place instead of scattering them, which makes his book easier to study. He held that narrators living in the same period with the possibility of meeting is enough, without proof of an actual meeting. His introduction is a short treatise on hadith method and is still read on its own.

sunan.s: A hadith book arranged by the chapters of fiqh, gathering the reports a jurist needs.
sunan.l: The four Sunan among the six books are those of Abu Dawud, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Majah, and in its own way al-Tirmidhi. Unlike the two Sahihs they include weak reports, usually with a remark, because their purpose is to lay out the evidence on each legal question rather than to collect only what is sound. Reading them well means reading the author's comments, not only the texts.

jami.s: A hadith book that covers every subject, not only law: belief, manners, tafsir, history and more.
jami.l: The word means gatherer. Sahih al-Bukhari and Jami' al-Tirmidhi are both jami' works. Al-Tirmidhi's is unusual in that he comments on nearly every hadith, names who else narrated it, and records which scholars acted on it, which makes it a teaching book as much as a collection.

muwatta.s: Malik ibn Anas's early collection, mixing hadith with Companion practice and the settled custom of Madinah.
muwatta.l: The name suggests something made smooth, or well trodden. It is the earliest of these books to survive in wide use, and it is a law book as much as a hadith book: Malik records a report, then how the people of Madinah actually acted. Al-Shafi'i is quoted as calling it the soundest book on earth after the Book of Allah, a judgement made before the two Sahihs were compiled.

musannaf.s: A collection arranged by legal topic that includes Companion and follower statements alongside hadith.
musannaf.l: The two great examples are the Musannaf of Abd al-Razzaq al-San'ani and that of Ibn Abi Shayba. They are enormous, and they are the main window onto what the earliest generations actually practised. Unlike a musnad, arranged by narrator, a musannaf is arranged by subject.

mustadrak.s: Al-Hakim's supplement, gathering hadiths he judged to meet the standards of al-Bukhari and Muslim.
mustadrak.l: A mustadrak is a book that makes up what an earlier author left out. Al-Hakim al-Naysaburi compiled his late in life and never finally revised it, and later scholars including al-Dhahabi found him lenient. A grading of sahih from al-Hakim alone is therefore treated as a starting point for checking rather than as a settled verdict.

arbain-nawawi.s: Al-Nawawi's short collection of foundational hadiths, the first hadith text most students memorise.
arbain-nawawi.l: It is called the Forty and usually contains forty two, since al-Nawawi added a couple beyond his original count. He chose reports that each carry a large share of the religion, opening with the hadith on intention. Ibn Rajab al-Hanbali added eight more and wrote the standard commentary, Jami' al-Ulum wa al-Hikam.

riyad-al-salihin.s: Al-Nawawi's topical collection on character and worship, the hadith book most widely read by ordinary Muslims.
riyad-al-salihin.l: The title means the gardens of the righteous. He drew almost entirely on the well known collections, opened each chapter with verses of the Qur'an, and arranged the whole book around how a person should live rather than around legal chapters. A small number of its reports are weak, and modern critical editions mark these.

kutub-arbaah.s: The four main hadith collections of Twelver Shia Islam, a separate corpus from the Sunni six books.
kutub-arbaah.l: They are al-Kafi by al-Kulayni, Man la yahduruhu al-Faqih by Ibn Babawayh, and al-Tahdhib and al-Istibsar by al-Tusi. They record reports from the Prophet and from the Imams, whose sayings carry authority in that tradition. The grading vocabulary overlaps with the Sunni one without matching it: a chain is judged partly by whether its narrators held the Imami creed, and the term muwaththaq marks a reliable narrator who did not.

amal-ahl-al-madinah.s: The living practice of Madinah, treated by Malik as evidence that can outweigh a single chain report.
amal-ahl-al-madinah.l: Malik's argument was that an act performed by a whole city in the Prophet's own town, generation after generation, reaches us by mass practice rather than by one man's memory. The Malikis therefore give it weight in law. The other three schools do not accept it as binding and give priority to the authentic report. The disagreement is about how transmission works, not about respect for the Sunnah.

salah.s: The formal Muslim prayer, performed five times a day at set times, facing Makkah.
salah.l: The word means connection and supplication. Salah is a fixed sequence of standing, bowing, prostrating and sitting, with recitation from the Qur'an, done at five appointed times between dawn and night. It is the second pillar of Islam and the first act a person is asked about on the Day of Judgement. Persian and Urdu speakers usually call it namaz, which is the same thing.

five-daily-prayers.s: The five obligatory prayers: dawn, past midday, afternoon, just after sunset, and night.
five-daily-prayers.l: Fajr runs from true dawn until sunrise. Dhuhr begins once the sun has passed its highest point. Asr fills the later afternoon, Maghrib begins at sunset, and Isha begins once the twilight has gone and lasts until dawn. The schools differ over exactly when Asr begins, and over which twilight closes the time of Maghrib, which is why mosques in the same city sometimes call these times an hour apart.

rakah.s: One complete unit of prayer: a standing, a bowing, and two prostrations.
rakah.l: Prayers are counted in rak'ahs. Fajr is two, Maghrib is three, and Dhuhr, Asr and Isha are four each. Within one rak'ah you stand and recite, bow, rise, prostrate, sit, and prostrate again. The plural is raka'at, which is why you will hear both forms.

qiyam.s: The standing part of the prayer, where al-Fatihah and other verses are recited.
qiyam.l: Qiyam simply means standing. Standing is required in obligatory prayers for anyone able to do it; someone who cannot stand prays sitting, and someone who cannot sit prays lying down, with no loss of reward. The same word appears in qiyam al-layl, meaning standing in prayer through the night.

ruku.s: The bowing in prayer, hands on the knees, back level, praising Allah's greatness.
ruku.l: From the standing position you bow with the back straight and the hands resting on the knees, saying subhana rabbiyal azim, glory to my Lord the Magnificent. The Qur'an repeatedly commands the believers to bow, and the posture is one of the pillars of the prayer without which a rak'ah does not count.

sujud.s: The prostration, forehead and nose on the ground, done twice in every rak'ah.
sujud.l: Seven parts touch the ground: the forehead with the nose, the two palms, the two knees, and the toes of both feet. The Prophet said a servant is nearest to his Lord in sujud, and told us to make much supplication there. It is the posture the whole prayer is built around, not a formality between recitations.

tashahhud.s: The words said while sitting in prayer, testifying to faith and greeting the Prophet.
tashahhud.l: The name comes from shahadah, testimony, because the words contain the declaration of faith. It is said in the sitting after the second rak'ah and again at the end of the prayer, where salawat on the Prophet is added before the closing salam. Several wordings are authentically reported, and mosques in different regions use different ones; all of them are sound.

taslim.s: The closing greeting of peace, turned to the right then the left, that ends the prayer.
taslim.l: You say as-salamu alaykum wa rahmatullah while turning the face to the right shoulder, then repeat it to the left. Until the taslim you are still in prayer and its restrictions apply. Some schools treat only the first salam as obligatory and the second as recommended.

takbir.s: The opening "Allahu akbar" that begins the prayer and closes off everything outside it.
takbir.l: Ihram here means entering a sanctified state, the same root as the pilgrim's ihram. Once you say the opening takbir, eating, speaking and turning away are no longer permitted until the closing salam. Smaller takbirs then mark each change of posture through the prayer.

niyyah.s: The intention in the heart that turns an ordinary act into an act of worship.
niyyah.l: Every act of worship needs a niyyah, and the Prophet said actions are only by intentions. It lives in the heart, so knowing which prayer you have stood up for is already the intention. The schools differ over whether saying it aloud helps: Shafi'is and Hanbalis allow it as an aid to focus, Malikis prefer it left unsaid, and none of them count the spoken words as the intention itself.

khushu.s: Stillness of the body and attention of the heart during prayer.
khushu.l: The Qur'an opens its description of successful believers with those who have khushu' in their prayer. It is not an emotion you must manufacture; it is mainly the practice of returning your attention each time it wanders, and of not fidgeting. Losing focus does not invalidate the prayer, which is why nobody should stop praying out of a feeling that their prayer is not good enough.

qunut.s: A supplication said standing in prayer, most often in witr or in times of crisis.
qunut.l: The word means devout standing. The schools place it differently: Hanafis say it in witr all year, Shafi'is in the dawn prayer and in witr in the second half of Ramadan, Malikis in the dawn prayer, and Hanbalis in witr. Most also recognise qunut an-nazilah, a supplication added during public calamity. Its wording is not fixed, so a person may ask in their own words.

witr.s: An odd-numbered night prayer, usually one or three rak'ahs, that closes the night.
witr.l: Witr means odd, as opposed to even. It is prayed any time after Isha until dawn, and the Prophet told his companions to make it the last prayer of their night. Hanafis classify it as wajib, close to obligatory; the other three schools call it a confirmed sunnah. Someone who intends to pray tahajjud usually delays witr until after it.

tahajjud.s: Voluntary prayer in the night, traditionally after sleeping and before dawn.
tahajjud.l: The root means to give up sleep. The Qur'an addresses the Prophet directly about it, and the last third of the night is its best time. There is no fixed number of rak'ahs; two is enough. Qiyam al-layl is a broader term for any prayer of the night, and in ordinary use the two words are treated as the same thing.

duha.s: A voluntary prayer of two to eight rak'ahs in the mid-morning, after sunrise and before noon.
duha.l: Its time opens once the sun has risen clearly above the horizon and closes shortly before midday. The Prophet described a charity due from every joint in the body each morning, and said two rak'ahs of duha are enough for all of it. Some call the earliest part of that window ishraq, and in the subcontinent it is often called chasht.

tarawih.s: The night prayer of Ramadan, prayed in congregation after Isha through the month.
tarawih.l: The name comes from the pauses for rest taken after every four rak'ahs. The number differs by custom and school: twenty rak'ahs became the settled practice of most schools and thirty six the old practice of Madinah, while many mosques pray eight, following reports of the Prophet's own night prayer. The number is not the point of the argument it is often made into; both are within the tradition.

sunnah-rawatib.s: The regular voluntary prayers attached before or after the five obligatory ones.
sunnah-rawatib.l: Twelve rak'ahs are reported as the standing pattern: two before Fajr, four before and two after Dhuhr, two after Maghrib, and two after Isha. The two before Fajr were the ones the Prophet never left. Any voluntary prayer outside this pattern is called nafl, and it carries no blame if missed.

jumuah.s: The Friday congregational prayer: a sermon followed by two rak'ahs, replacing Dhuhr.
jumuah.l: The Qur'an commands believers to leave off trade and hurry to the remembrance of Allah when the Friday call is made. It is obligatory on adult resident men who are able to attend, and not obligatory on women, travellers or the sick, though all may attend. Whoever misses it prays Dhuhr as normal.

khutbah.s: The sermon given before the Friday prayer and after the two Eid prayers.
khutbah.l: The Friday khutbah comes in two parts with a brief sitting between them, and it is delivered before the prayer, not after. Scholars explain it as standing in place of two of the four Dhuhr rak'ahs, so listening to it is part of the worship, and most hold that talking while it is delivered is forbidden. The Eid khutbah works the other way round: it follows the prayer, and staying for it is recommended rather than required.

salat-al-eid.s: The two rak'ah prayer on the morning of the two Eids, with extra takbirs and a sermon after.
salat-al-eid.l: It is prayed in the mid-morning, in congregation, without adhan or iqamah, and the number of added takbirs differs by school. Rulings on it differ too: Hanafis call it wajib, Hanbalis a communal obligation, Shafi'is and Malikis a confirmed sunnah. Praying it in an open space rather than inside the mosque is the older practice.

salat-al-janazah.s: The funeral prayer, said standing over the deceased, with no bowing and no prostration.
salat-al-janazah.l: It consists of four takbirs said while standing: al-Fatihah in the Shafi'i and Hanbali schools and praise of Allah in the Hanafi and Maliki, then salawat on the Prophet, then supplication for the deceased, then the closing salam. It is a communal obligation, meaning that if enough people pray it the duty is lifted from the rest. It is a prayer for the dead person, not a ceremony for the family, which is why it is kept short.

istikharah.s: Two voluntary rak'ahs followed by a supplication asking Allah to choose the better of two paths.
istikharah.l: The word means asking for the good. The Prophet taught it for ordinary decisions, and it is prayed once you already have an inclination, not instead of thinking and asking advice. A common misunderstanding is that it must produce a dream or a sign; it does not. You pray, you decide, and you trust the outcome you are given.

qasr.s: Shortening the four-rak'ah prayers to two while travelling, and combining two prayers in one time.
qasr.l: The Qur'an mentions shortening prayer on a journey, and the Prophet did it consistently. Qasr applies to Dhuhr, Asr and Isha only; Fajr and Maghrib are never shortened. Jam' is a separate concession, joining Dhuhr with Asr or Maghrib with Isha. The schools set different thresholds for how far you must travel and how long you may stay before you pray in full again.

jamaah.s: Praying together behind one imam, which multiplies the reward of the prayer many times over.
jamaah.l: The Prophet said congregational prayer surpasses praying alone by twenty seven degrees. Two people are enough to form a jama'ah. The schools differ on how binding it is for men: Hanbalis hold it individually obligatory, Shafi'is a communal obligation, and Hanafis and Malikis a confirmed sunnah. Someone who joins late catches up alone after the imam finishes.

imam.s: The person who leads the prayer, standing in front while the rows follow his movements.
imam.l: The word means one who is in front. The Prophet said the person who leads should be the one who knows most Qur'an, then the most learned in the sunnah. Any competent adult man can lead; it is not a clerical office or a job title, and most mosques employ one only for convenience. In wider usage imam also names a great scholar, as in Imam Malik, and in Shia Islam it carries a specific and much larger meaning.

adhan.s: The call announcing that a prayer time has entered, given aloud before each obligatory prayer.
adhan.l: It was taught to the companions in Madinah after they discussed how to gather people, and Bilal was its first caller. Its lines declare Allah's greatness, the testimony of faith, and the summons to prayer and to success. The Fajr adhan adds the line that prayer is better than sleep. The one who calls it is the muezzin.

iqamah.s: The second, shorter call given immediately before the congregation starts the prayer.
iqamah.l: Its words are almost those of the adhan, with the added line qad qamat as-salah, the prayer has begun. Hanafis repeat its phrases as in the adhan; the other three schools say most of them once. It is also given, quietly, by a person praying alone, and the schools differ over how binding it is.

qiblah.s: The direction of the Kaaba in Makkah, which Muslims face when they pray.
qiblah.l: For sixteen or seventeen months in Madinah the Muslims prayed towards Jerusalem, and in the second year after the hijrah the Qur'an turned them to the Sacred Mosque. Those far from Makkah are asked for the direction rather than a perfect line, and someone with no way of knowing prays towards their best judgement and the prayer counts. Mosques mark it with a niche called the mihrab.

sujud-al-sahw.s: Two extra prostrations that repair a mistake made by forgetting during the prayer.
sujud-al-sahw.l: They cover adding a posture, leaving out a required part, or losing count. The Prophet said that when a person is unsure, he should settle on the lower number and make the two prostrations. The schools place them differently, before or after the closing salam depending on the kind of mistake, so follow what your local imam does rather than assuming an error.

sujud-al-tilawah.s: A single prostration made when reciting or hearing one of the Qur'an's verses of prostration.
sujud-al-tilawah.l: Copies of the Qur'an mark these verses in the margin. Depending on the school they are counted as eleven, fourteen or fifteen. It is one prostration, done inside or outside prayer, and it is recommended rather than required for most scholars. A related act is sujud ash-shukr, a prostration of thanks on receiving good news.

qada-al-fawait.s: Performing an obligatory act of worship after its proper time has passed, to make it up.
qada-al-fawait.l: The Qur'an tells whoever is ill or travelling in Ramadan to fast the same number of other days, which is the clearest case of qada. Missed prayers are made up as soon as one is able, in order where practical, and there is no need to announce or dramatise it. Someone with years of missed prayers is usually advised to add a few to each day rather than attempt to clear them at once.

taharah.s: Ritual purity, the state a person must be in before praying and, for most scholars, before touching the Qur'an.
taharah.l: Books of fiqh almost always begin with taharah, because it is the gate to everything else. It has two sides: removing physical filth from the body, clothes and place of prayer, and lifting the ritual states that block worship. The Prophet called purification half of faith, and the Qur'an says Allah loves those who keep themselves pure.

wudu.s: The washing done before prayer: face, arms to the elbows, wiping the head, and feet to the ankles.
wudu.l: The four acts are named directly in the Qur'an, and the Prophet added rinsing the mouth and nose, washing the hands first, and doing each part three times. Wudu is broken by using the toilet, by passing wind, and by deep sleep; it is not broken by touching an animal or by ordinary dirt. One wudu lasts for as many prayers as you like until something breaks it.

ghusl.s: The full washing of the whole body that lifts the major state of ritual impurity.
ghusl.l: It is required after intercourse or sexual discharge, and at the end of menstruation and postnatal bleeding. It is recommended before Jumu'ah, the two Eids, and entering ihram. At minimum it is an intention and water reaching every part of the skin and hair; the schools differ over whether rinsing the mouth and nose, and rubbing the skin, are obligatory or recommended. A ghusl done properly also counts for wudu.

tayammum.s: Purification with clean earth instead of water, when water is unavailable or would cause harm.
tayammum.l: You strike clean ground or dust with the palms and wipe the face and the hands. The Qur'an permits it for the traveller, the ill, and anyone who cannot find water. It stands in for both wudu and ghusl, and it ends the moment water becomes usable again. It is a real concession, not a lesser or shameful substitute.

najasah.s: A substance counted as ritually impure, which must be removed from body, clothes and prayer place.
najasah.l: Urine, faeces, blood, pork and wine are the agreed cases. Water removes najasah once the colour, taste and smell are gone. The schools differ over particular cases, such as dogs, and over how small a trace is overlooked. Najasah is about the substance; the state of a person needing wudu or ghusl is hadath, and the two are often confused.

hadath.s: The ritual state that blocks prayer until it is lifted by wudu or by ghusl.
hadath.l: Minor hadath comes from things like using the toilet or sleeping deeply, and is lifted by wudu. Major hadath comes from sexual discharge, menstruation and postnatal bleeding, and is lifted by ghusl. It is a legal state, not dirt: a person in hadath may be perfectly clean, and a person covered in mud may have valid wudu.

janabah.s: The state following intercourse or sexual discharge, lifted only by a full ghusl.
janabah.l: A person in this state is called junub. Until they wash, prayer and tawaf are not performed and, for most scholars, the Qur'an is not recited or carried. The Qur'an mentions it plainly alongside the verse on wudu, and there is nothing shameful in it; it is simply a state with a known remedy. If water is unavailable, tayammum stands in for the ghusl.

hayd.s: Menstruation, during which prayer and fasting are lifted and intimacy is paused.
hayd.l: Prayers missed in these days are not made up, but fasts of Ramadan are. Nifas is the parallel state of bleeding after childbirth and carries the same rulings. Bleeding outside these two, called istihadah, does not excuse prayer or fasting. The schools differ over the minimum and maximum days of hayd, which changes when a woman resumes worship, so local guidance matters here.

masah-al-khuffayn.s: Wiping over footwear in wudu instead of washing the feet, once they were put on in purity.
masah-al-khuffayn.l: The permission is very widely reported from the Prophet. It lasts one day and night for a resident and three days and nights for a traveller, counted from the first wipe after wudu was broken. It ends with ghusl or with taking the socks off. Whether ordinary cotton socks qualify or only thick leather ones is an old and continuing discussion among scholars.

siwak.s: A twig used to clean the teeth, recommended before prayer, wudu, and on waking.
siwak.l: It is cut from the arak tree, softened at one end into bristles. The Prophet said that were it not a hardship, he would have ordered it before every prayer. It is a sunnah of cleanliness rather than a condition of anything, and a toothbrush achieves most of the same purpose for anyone who has no arak wood.

sawm.s: Fasting: abstaining from food, drink and intimacy from true dawn until sunset, with intention.
sawm.l: The word means to hold back. Fasting the month of Ramadan is the fourth pillar, and voluntary fasts are kept on other days through the year. The Qur'an sets its purpose as taqwa, God consciousness, and the Prophet warned that a fast without leaving off false speech is only hunger and thirst. Illness, travel, pregnancy, nursing, menstruation and old age all carry recognised concessions.

suhur.s: The meal eaten before dawn to begin a day of fasting.
suhur.l: The name comes from sahar, the last darkness before dawn. The Prophet said to eat it because there is blessing in it, and encouraged delaying it until close to the dawn. It is a sunnah rather than a condition, so a fast is still valid if a person sleeps through it.

iftar.s: Breaking the fast at sunset, traditionally with dates and water before the Maghrib prayer.
iftar.l: The Prophet hastened it rather than delaying it, and said people remain in good as long as they do so. He broke his fast with fresh dates, or dry dates, or else a drink of water. Feeding a fasting person their iftar is described as earning the same reward as their fast, which is the origin of the communal iftar tables.

itikaf.s: Staying in a mosque for a set period, devoted to worship and cut off from ordinary business.
itikaf.l: The word means to keep to something. The Qur'an mentions it in the verses on fasting, and the Prophet kept i'tikaf in the last ten nights of Ramadan every year. The one in retreat leaves only for necessity. Hanafis allow a woman to observe it in the place she prays at home; the other schools hold that it must be in a mosque.

kaffarah.s: A fixed expiation owed for certain deliberate breaches, heavier than simply making the act up.
kaffarah.l: For deliberately breaking a Ramadan fast, the expiation is to fast sixty consecutive days, or if unable, to feed sixty poor people, alongside making up the day. Hanafis and Malikis apply this to deliberate eating and drinking as well as intercourse; Shafi'is and Hanbalis restrict it to intercourse. A separate and much lighter kaffarah exists for breaking an oath. It is not owed by someone who broke the fast by mistake or out of genuine need.

fidyah.s: Feeding a poor person for each fast that a person is permanently unable to keep or make up.
fidyah.l: The Qur'an mentions it for those who can only fast with great hardship, which scholars apply to the very old and the chronically ill with no prospect of recovery. It is one meal or its value for each missed day, given to someone in need. Anyone who expects to recover owes qada instead, and should not pay fidyah to avoid fasting.

zakat.s: The yearly obligatory share of qualifying wealth, normally 2.5 percent, given to those entitled to it.
zakat.l: The word carries both purification and growth. Zakat is the third pillar, and the Qur'an names it beside the prayer again and again. It is due on savings, gold, silver and trade goods held for a lunar year above the nisab, at one fortieth of their value, while crops, livestock and mined wealth have their own rates. It is a debt owed to specific people, not a donation the giver may direct wherever they wish.

nisab.s: The minimum amount of wealth a person must hold before zakat becomes due on it.
nisab.l: It is set by the Prophet's rulings at about 85 grams of gold or about 595 grams of silver, with slightly different weights reported. Scholars differ over which standard to apply to cash: the silver figure is much lower, so it brings more people into zakat and gives more to the poor, while the gold figure sets a higher threshold and is widely used today. Below the nisab, no zakat is owed and nothing is blameworthy.

hawl.s: The full lunar year that wealth must be held above the nisab before zakat falls due on it.
hawl.l: You set a date, usually a day in Ramadan for ease of memory, and pay on whatever qualifying wealth you hold on that date each year. Hanafis fold money that comes and goes during the year into that one date; the other schools start a fresh year for wealth newly acquired. Crops are the exception: their zakat is due at harvest, and buried treasure is due at once.

zakat-al-fitr.s: A small measure of staple food given for every household member before the Eid al-Fitr prayer.
zakat-al-fitr.l: The Prophet made it obligatory on every Muslim, young and old, free and owned, as a purification for the fasting person and food for the poor. The measure is one sa', roughly two and a half to three kilograms of the local staple. Hanafis permit paying its value in money, which most charities now do; the other schools generally require the food itself. Given after the Eid prayer it counts as ordinary charity, so it is paid early.

sadaqah.s: Voluntary giving, of any amount and at any time, to anyone in need.
sadaqah.l: The root is sidq, truthfulness, because giving is treated as proof that a claim to faith is real. Unlike zakat it has no threshold, no fixed rate and no fixed recipients. The Prophet counted removing harm from a path, a good word, and a smile as sadaqah, so it is not limited to money. Giving quietly is described in the Qur'an as better than giving openly.

sadaqah-jariyah.s: A charity that keeps benefiting people, so its reward continues after the giver dies.
sadaqah-jariyah.l: Jariyah means flowing. The Prophet said that when a person dies their deeds stop except for three, and named ongoing charity, knowledge that others benefit from, and a righteous child who prays for them. A well, a tree, a school and a copy of the Qur'an left for others are the classic examples. Endowing property permanently for this purpose is called waqf.

asnaf.s: The eight groups the Qur'an names as the only lawful recipients of zakat.
asnaf.l: They are the poor, the needy, those employed to collect it, those whose hearts are to be reconciled, freeing those in bondage, the debt burdened, the cause of Allah, and the stranded traveller. The list is fixed by a single verse, which is why most scholars hold that zakat cannot be spent on a mosque building or a general good cause the way sadaqah can. Scholars differ over how widely the seventh category may be read.

khums.s: A fifth of certain wealth; in Sunni law on spoils and treasure, in Shia practice a yearly payment.
khums.l: The Qur'an assigns a fifth of the spoils of war to named recipients, and Sunni schools extend this to rikaz, wealth found buried in the ground. Twelver Shia jurisprudence reads the verse far more broadly, as a fifth of a person's yearly surplus income, paid through a marja' and divided between the share of the Imam and the descendants of the Prophet. A reader meeting the word in a Shia context is meeting this second meaning.

hajj.s: The pilgrimage to Makkah in Dhul Hijjah, obligatory once in a lifetime on those who are able.
hajj.l: It is the fifth pillar. The condition of ability, called istita'ah, covers health, safe passage and the money to travel and to leave dependants provided for; someone who lacks these owes nothing. The rites run over several days across Makkah, Mina, Arafah and Muzdalifah, retracing the acts of Ibrahim, Hajar and Isma'il. Umrah can be done at any time of year, but hajj cannot.

umrah.s: The lesser pilgrimage: ihram, tawaf, sa'i and cutting the hair, and it may be done any time of year.
umrah.l: It shares its rites with hajj but has no Arafah, no Mina and no fixed date. It takes a few hours rather than several days. Shafi'is and Hanbalis hold umrah obligatory once in a lifetime; Hanafis and Malikis call it a confirmed sunnah. Performing it in Ramadan is described in a well known hadith as equal in reward to a hajj, which does not remove the obligation of hajj itself.

ihram.s: The sanctified state a pilgrim enters with intention and talbiyah, marked by simple unsewn dress.
ihram.l: The root means to make something forbidden, because entering it makes ordinary permissible things off limits. Men wear two unsewn white cloths; women wear ordinary modest clothing with the face and hands uncovered, and there is no special ihram dress for them. The common misunderstanding is that the towels are the ihram; they are not, and a person who has made the intention is in ihram whatever they happen to be wearing.

mahzurat-al-ihram.s: The things forbidden while in ihram, such as perfume, cutting hair or nails, hunting and intimacy.
mahzurat-al-ihram.l: The Qur'an forbids sexual relations, wrongdoing and arguing during hajj, and forbids hunting land game while in ihram. To these are added perfume, cutting hair or nails, and for men sewn clothing and covering the head; most schools add contracting a marriage, which Hanafis permit. Breaking one out of forgetfulness is not sinful, though the schools differ over whether compensation is still owed, and doing it deliberately usually carries a dam or a fidyah of fasting, feeding or a sacrifice.

miqat.s: The fixed boundary points where a pilgrim must enter ihram before continuing towards Makkah.
miqat.l: The Prophet named four, one on each approach: Dhul Hulayfah for Madinah, al-Juhfah for Syria and Egypt, Qarn al-Manazil for Najd, and Yalamlam for Yemen. Dhat Irq, for those coming from Iraq, was fixed by Umar, and some report it from the Prophet as well. Anyone travelling through one, including passengers on a flight passing over it, enters ihram there or before. There is also a miqat in time: the months of hajj, Shawwal, Dhul Qa'dah and the first days of Dhul Hijjah.

talbiyah.s: The pilgrim's answering call, beginning labbayk Allahumma labbayk, here I am, my Lord, here I am.
talbiyah.l: It continues: no partner have You, here I am, all praise and favour are Yours, and the dominion, You have no partner. It is said on entering ihram and repeated on the road, aloud by men and quietly by women. It is an answer to the summons the Qur'an says Ibrahim was told to proclaim. On umrah pilgrims stop when they begin the tawaf; on hajj the talbiyah continues until the stoning on the tenth.

tawaf.s: Circling the Kaaba seven times, keeping it on your left, starting and ending at the Black Stone.
tawaf.l: The Qur'an commands circling the Ancient House. Most schools require the pilgrim to be in a state of purity, and Hanafis count a tawaf made without wudu as valid but owing a dam. Each circuit begins and ends at the corner of the Black Stone. Hajj has up to three: tawaf al-qudum on arrival, tawaf al-ifadah after Arafah which is a pillar of the hajj, and tawaf al-wada as a farewell before leaving Makkah. There is no obligation to touch or kiss the stone; most pilgrims simply point to it.

sai.s: Walking seven times between the hills of Safa and Marwah, beginning at Safa and ending at Marwah.
sai.l: It retraces Hajar's search for water for her infant son Isma'il, which ended with the spring of Zamzam. Each single crossing counts as one, so the seventh brings you to Marwah. The Qur'an names the two hills among the symbols of Allah. Men jog lightly between the two green markers, where the valley floor once lay; women walk throughout.

wuquf.s: Standing at Arafah on the ninth of Dhul Hijjah, the one rite without which there is no hajj.
wuquf.l: The Prophet said the hajj is Arafah. A pilgrim who reaches any part of the plain within its window has performed it, whether standing, sitting or asleep, and one who misses it has missed the hajj that year. The majority date the window from midday until dawn of the next day; Hanbalis start it at dawn on the ninth. The day is spent in supplication rather than in any set ritual.

arafah.s: The open plain east of Makkah where pilgrims gather on the ninth of Dhul Hijjah.
arafah.l: The small hill within it is called Jabal ar-Rahmah, the mount of mercy, and the farewell sermon was delivered nearby. Its day is the climax of the hajj. For Muslims not on hajj, fasting the day of Arafah is a strongly recommended sunnah described as expiating the year before and the year after; pilgrims themselves do not fast it.

muzdalifah.s: The open ground between Arafah and Mina where pilgrims spend the night of the tenth.
muzdalifah.l: The Qur'an calls it al-Mash'ar al-Haram, the Sacred Monument. Pilgrims arrive after sunset, pray Maghrib and Isha together, sleep on the ground under the sky, and gather pebbles for the stoning. The weak, the elderly and those accompanying them may move on to Mina in the later part of the night, a concession the Prophet gave to his own family.

mina.s: The valley near Makkah where pilgrims camp before Arafah and for the days after Eid.
mina.l: Pilgrims stay there on the eighth of Dhul Hijjah, called the day of tarwiyah, then return on the tenth after Arafah and remain for the days of tashriq, the eleventh to the thirteenth. The three jamarat stand at its edge. A pilgrim may leave after the twelfth if they depart before sunset; otherwise the thirteenth is completed.

jamarat.s: The three pillars at Mina that pilgrims pelt with small pebbles, called ramy.
jamarat.l: They mark the places where Ibrahim is said to have driven away the whisperer as he went to fulfil his command. On the tenth only the largest, Jamrat al-Aqabah, is stoned with seven pebbles; on the following days all three are stoned in order. The pebbles are the size of a chickpea, and the act is a symbol of refusal, not an attack on a physical devil. Those unable to go may appoint someone to stone on their behalf.

hady.s: The animal offered in Makkah by pilgrims performing tamattu' or qiran, and its meat given away.
hady.l: The word means a gift brought forward. It is a sheep or goat per pilgrim, or a seventh share of a camel or cow, slaughtered after the stoning on the tenth. The Qur'an says neither the meat nor the blood reaches Allah, only the God consciousness of the giver. It is different from the qurbani offered by Muslims everywhere at Eid, and different again from a dam owed as compensation.

halq.s: Shaving the head after the rites, which releases the pilgrim from the state of ihram.
halq.l: The Prophet asked mercy for those who shave three times and for those who trim once, so shaving is the better of the two for men. Women never shave; they gather their hair and cut about a fingertip's length from the end. It is done after the stoning on the tenth for hajj, and after the sa'i for umrah.

taqsir.s: Trimming the hair rather than shaving it, the alternative way to leave ihram.
taqsir.l: Most schools require a little to be taken from all around the head rather than a single snip from one place. It is the option chosen by women, and by men who wish to keep hair for a shave at the end of a hajj that follows soon after. Both halq and taqsir close the rites of umrah, and no further trimming is needed after that.

tahallul.s: Coming out of ihram, so that what was forbidden during it becomes permitted again.
tahallul.l: In hajj it happens in two stages. The first comes after stoning Jamrat al-Aqabah and cutting the hair: normal clothes and perfume return, but intimacy does not. The second comes after tawaf al-ifadah and its sa'i, and lifts everything. In umrah there is only one, after the hair is cut.

dam.s: A compensating sacrifice owed for omitting a required rite of hajj or breaking a rule of ihram.
dam.l: The word means blood. It is usually a sheep or goat, slaughtered in the sanctuary and given to the poor there, and for some breaches a person may instead fast or feed the needy. The schools differ over which acts are required rather than recommended, so an omission that costs a dam in one school may cost nothing in another. A dam repairs a shortfall; a hady is part of the pilgrimage itself.

tamattu.s: One of the three ways to perform hajj: umrah first, then leaving ihram, then hajj from Makkah.
tamattu.l: In tamattu' you complete umrah, come out of ihram and wait, then enter ihram again for hajj on the eighth. In qiran you hold both in a single unbroken ihram, and in ifrad you perform hajj alone. Tamattu' and qiran require a hady; ifrad does not. The schools differ over which is best, and tamattu' is what most pilgrims on organised trips perform.

quran.s: The speech of Allah revealed to Muhammad in Arabic over about twenty three years, preserved word for word.
quran.l: The word means the recitation, from a root meaning to read aloud. It is one book of 114 surahs, revealed piece by piece between Makkah and Madinah, memorised by the Companions and written down in the Prophet's lifetime. Muslims hold that the Arabic wording is itself the revelation, which is why any rendering into another language is called a translation of the meaning and never the Qur'an.

ulum-al-quran.s: The family of disciplines that study how the Qur'an was revealed, collected, recited, read and interpreted.
ulum-al-quran.l: It covers revelation and its occasions, Makkan and Madinan passages, the canonical readings, abrogation, the clear and the ambiguous, and the rules of interpretation. It is the map you are meant to have before opening a work of tafsir. The two classic reference works are al-Zarkashi's al-Burhan and al-Suyuti's al-Itqan.

mushaf.s: A physical copy of the Qur'an: the pages, ink and binding, as distinct from the revelation itself.
mushaf.l: The word comes from sahifah, a written sheet, so a mushaf is the sheets gathered between two covers. Muslims keep the distinction: the Qur'an is the speech of Allah, the mushaf is the object you can drop or tear. Worn out copies are not put in the bin; they are buried or burned in a clean place. Uthman burned the copies his standard edition replaced, and later scholars differ over which of the two is better.

ayah.s: A verse of the Qur'an, and in ordinary Arabic a sign.
ayah.l: The same word is used for the signs of Allah in creation, which is why a verse is called a sign rather than a line. Most scholars hold that verse endings were fixed by the Prophet's own recitation; the numbers printed in the margins were added later as an aid. The Hafs printing counts 6,236 verses, and other counting traditions divide a few verses differently and reach slightly different totals.

surah.s: A chapter of the Qur'an; there are 114, arranged in the mushaf rather than by date of revelation.
surah.l: Each surah has a name, usually taken from a striking word inside it, and every surah except at-Tawbah opens with the basmalah. They range from al-Baqarah at 286 verses down to al-Kawthar at three. The order in the mushaf is not the order of revelation, so many of the short surahs at the end are among the earliest to come down.

juz.s: One of the thirty roughly equal parts the Qur'an is divided into, for reading it over a month.
juz.l: The division is a reading aid rather than part of the revelation, and it usually cuts across a surah rather than falling neatly between two. In South Asia a juz is called a para or sipara. Reading one juz a day completes the whole Qur'an in a month, which is why almost every Ramadan schedule is built on it.

juz-amma.s: The thirtieth and last part of the Qur'an, running from Surah an-Naba to the end.
juz-amma.l: It is named after its first word, amma, in the opening verse of an-Naba. It holds thirty seven short surahs, the ones most used in prayer, so it is where children and new Muslims usually begin memorising. Small printed booklets of it are sold everywhere for exactly that reason.

hizb.s: Half a juz; the Qur'an is divided into sixty hizbs for steady daily reading.
hizb.l: The word means a share or portion, in the sense of a person's allotted reading. Each hizb is split again into four quarters, marked in the margin of most mushafs. In parts of North and West Africa the daily recitation of a mosque is organised around the hizb rather than the juz.

rub-al-hizb.s: A quarter of a hizb, shown by the small ornamental star in the margin of the mushaf.
rub-al-hizb.l: There are 240 of these quarters, four to each of the sixty hizbs. The symbol is a printer's mark added by later scholars so readers can keep their place and portion out a daily amount. It carries no ruling; nothing is said or done when you reach one.

manzil.s: One of seven divisions of the Qur'an, used by those who complete a full reading each week.
manzil.l: Companions are reported to have divided their reading this way, in portions of three, five, seven, nine, eleven and thirteen surahs, with the remainder of the mushaf as the seventh. It is an older habit than the thirty part division and is still followed by some. A separate booklet of protective verses is also called Manzil; it borrowed the name but is a different thing.

ruku-quran.s: A short thematic passage marked with a small ain in the margin, mostly in South Asian mushafs.
ruku-quran.l: The word is the same one used for bowing in prayer, because an imam would recite one such passage and then bow. It groups a handful of verses that hang together, which makes it a natural unit for tarawih and for memorising. It is a later reading aid and is absent from most Arab printings.

mufassal.s: The last stretch of the Qur'an, from about Surah Qaf to the end, made up of shorter surahs.
mufassal.l: The name means the frequently divided, because the basmalah separates its many short surahs so often. Scholars split it into long, middle and short sections, which is the language books of fiqh use when describing what to recite in each prayer. Where it begins is disputed: most say Surah Qaf, others say al-Hujurat.

huruf-muqattaat.s: The single letters that open twenty nine surahs, such as Alif Lam Mim, recited letter by letter.
huruf-muqattaat.l: They are read as separate letter names, not run together as a word. Many early scholars, Companions among them, said their meaning is known to Allah alone and stopped there. Others suggested they point at the challenge itself: this revelation is built from the very letters its opponents already had.

fatihah.s: The seven verse opening surah, recited in the prayer; most schools require it in every unit.
fatihah.l: Its names include the Opening, the Mother of the Book, and the seven oft repeated verses. It is a prayer spoken in the second person: praise first, then a single request, for guidance on the straight path. The schools differ over whether the basmalah counts as its first verse, which is why the seven verses are numbered differently in different mushafs. They differ again over whether someone praying behind an imam recites it: the Hanafis hold that the imam's recitation stands for him.

basmalah.s: The opening line In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful, found before nearly every surah.
basmalah.l: It stands at the head of 113 surahs; at-Tawbah alone has none. It also appears inside the Qur'an as the opening of Sulayman's letter in Surah an-Naml. The schools differ over whether it is a verse of al-Fatihah and whether it is said aloud in prayer, which is why practice varies from one mosque to the next.

istiadhah.s: Saying I seek refuge with Allah from the accursed Shaytan before beginning to recite.
istiadhah.l: The Qur'an instructs it directly: when you recite the Qur'an, seek refuge with Allah from Shaytan the rejected. It is said once at the start of a sitting, not before every verse, and it is not itself part of the Qur'an. Most scholars treat it as strongly recommended rather than obligatory.

sadaqallah.s: The phrase Allah the Magnificent has spoken the truth, often said on finishing a recitation.
sadaqallah.l: The words are true in themselves and echo a phrase in Surah Al Imran. What scholars differ over is treating them as a fixed ending that must always follow recitation, since neither the Prophet nor the early generations are known to have made a habit of it. Some call it a harmless custom, others discourage making it a rule; leaving it out is not a fault.

makki.s: A verse or surah revealed before the migration to Madinah, whatever place it came down in.
makki.l: The usual definition is by time rather than geography, so a verse revealed at Makkah during the farewell pilgrimage still counts as Madani. Makki passages tend to be shorter and more urgent, dealing with belief, resurrection and the earlier prophets, and often open with O mankind. Around eighty six surahs are classed as Makki, with several disputed.

madani.s: A verse or surah revealed after the migration to Madinah, whatever place it came down in.
madani.l: Madani passages generally deal with the shape of a community: law, family, treaties, warfare, hypocrisy and the People of the Book, and they often open with O you who believe. Their verses are usually longer. Around twenty eight surahs are classed as Madani, and for a few the classification is contested or mixed.

nuzul-al-quran.s: The sending down of the Qur'an: gradually, over roughly twenty three years, alongside real events.
nuzul-al-quran.l: The first revelation was Iqra, in the cave of Hira, and the last verses came near the end of the Prophet's life. The Qur'an explains its own slow pace: it came in stages to steady the Prophet's heart. A well known report from Ibn Abbas adds an earlier stage, the whole Qur'an brought down to the lowest heaven on Laylat al-Qadr and then released piece by piece.

asbab-an-nuzul.s: The event or question a particular verse was revealed in answer to.
