asbab-an-nuzul.l: Knowing the occasion often makes a verse click into place, and it guards against reading a narrow ruling as a sweeping one. These occasions reach us only through narrations, so they are weighed like any report, and a great many verses have no occasion attached at all. The working rule for most scholars is that the lesson lies in the general wording, not in the particular incident.

jam-al-quran.s: The gathering of the Qur'an into one written volume, carried out under Abu Bakr and then Uthman.
jam-al-quran.l: It was already written in the Prophet's lifetime on parchment, palm stalks and bone, and memorised by many Companions. After heavy losses among the reciters at the battle of Yamamah, Abu Bakr had Zayd ibn Thabit gather it into one set of sheets, which were later kept by Hafsah. Uthman then had standard copies made from those sheets and sent to the main cities, so that the whole community read from one text.

rasm-uthmani.s: The spelling of the Uthmanic copies, kept in mushafs even where it differs from modern Arabic spelling.
rasm-uthmani.l: The original copies carried no dots and no vowel marks, only the consonantal skeleton, which could hold more than one authentic reading at once. Later scholars added dots, vowels and stop marks without touching that skeleton. This is why some words are written in the mushaf differently from how they are written today, and why Uthmani and simplified Indo-Pak printings look unlike each other on the page.

ahruf-sabah.s: The seven modes in which the Qur'an was revealed, an ease for the community; what a mode is stays disputed.
ahruf-sabah.l: The Prophet said the Qur'an was sent down in seven ahruf, and the report appears in the most reliable collections. What an harf actually is has been argued over for centuries, with dozens of explanations offered and none settled. The ahruf are not the same thing as the ten qira'at, though the readings preserve part of what the ahruf allowed.

qiraat.s: The canonical ways of reciting the Qur'an, each carried by chain from the Prophet through a named reader.
qiraat.l: Ten readings are accepted as authentic, each passed on by two main transmitters, giving twenty transmissions in common use. The differences are small and mostly touch vowels, lengthening or a single letter; they rarely change meaning, and where they do the two meanings sit alongside each other rather than clash. A reading counts as authentic only if it has a sound chain, fits the Uthmanic skeleton and is valid Arabic.

hafs.s: The reading found in most printed mushafs today, transmitted by Hafs from his teacher Asim of Kufa.
hafs.l: Hafs ibn Sulayman learned it from Asim ibn Abi an-Najud, whose chain runs back through the Companions to the Prophet. It spread with mass printing and is now the default across most of the Muslim world, which is why many readers assume it is the only way the Qur'an is read. Asim's other transmitter, Shu'bah, differs from Hafs in a modest number of places.

warsh.s: The reading common in North and West Africa, transmitted by Warsh from Nafi of Madinah.
warsh.l: Uthman ibn Sa'id, nicknamed Warsh, took it from Nafi al-Madani, and it travelled west with the scholars of the Maghrib. Set beside Hafs it lengthens certain vowels further, handles some hamzahs more softly, and tilts some fathas towards a kasra. Nafi's other transmitter is Qalun, whose reading is used in Libya and parts of Tunisia.

ijazah-quran.s: A licence to teach a reading, granted after reciting the entire Qur'an to a qualified teacher.
ijazah-quran.l: The teacher listens to every letter, corrects it, and only then names the student in an unbroken chain of teachers reaching back to the Prophet. It certifies that you were heard, not that you passed a written exam. Most ijazahs given today are in Hafs from Asim, though teachers of the other readings still grant them.

mutun-tajwid.s: The beginner's tajwid poem students memorise, alongside al-Jazariyyah and, for the readings, ash-Shatibiyyah.
mutun-tajwid.l: Tuhfat al-Atfal, by al-Jamzuri, covers the rules of nun sakinah, meem sakinah and madd in about sixty lines of verse. Al-Jazariyyah, by Ibn al-Jazari, goes further into the articulation points and qualities of the letters. Ash-Shatibiyyah is the long poem behind the seven readings, and students normally reach it only after the first two are secure.

nasikh-mansukh.s: Abrogation: a later ruling replacing an earlier one, the abrogating verse and the abrogated verse.
nasikh-mansukh.l: The Qur'an raises the idea itself, and the clearest example is the change of qiblah from Jerusalem to the Kaaba. Early scholars listed hundreds of cases, often using the word loosely for any narrowing or qualifying of a general rule. Later scholars tightened the definition sharply, and Shah Waliullah held that only about five genuine cases remain; the count is still debated.

muhkam-mutashabih.s: The clear verses whose meaning is decisive, and the verses that can carry more than one meaning.
muhkam-mutashabih.l: The Qur'an draws the distinction itself, in Surah Al Imran, and warns against those who chase the ambiguous looking for discord. Muhkam verses are the backbone: the commands, the prohibitions, the plain statements. Mutashabih covers what is genuinely open to more than one reading, and matters of the unseen whose reality many scholars leave to Allah rather than forcing into a shape.

munasabah.s: The study of how verses and surahs connect, and why they sit in the order they do.
munasabah.l: It asks why one verse follows another, and how a surah opens and closes on the same note. Al-Biqa'i's Nazm ad-Durar is the largest classical work built entirely on this idea. Some early scholars were cautious about it, since the arrangement is a matter of revelation rather than an author ordering his chapters.

gharib-al-quran.s: The study of the Qur'an's rare or difficult words, and what they meant to their first hearers.
gharib-al-quran.l: Arabic shifts over time, and words that were everyday in the seventh century can be obscure now. Ibn Abbas is known for explaining such words by citing lines of pre Islamic poetry. Al-Raghib al-Isfahani's Mufradat is the standard reference and is still the first book a student opens on a hard word.

amthal-al-quran.s: The parables of the Qur'an: everyday images used to make an unseen truth visible.
amthal-al-quran.l: A spider's house for false reliance, a lamp in a niche for light upon light, ash scattered by the wind for deeds without faith. The Qur'an says it sets out such comparisons for people so that they may reflect. Reading them as pictures rather than as puzzles to decode is usually the point.

aqsam-al-quran.s: The oaths of the Qur'an, where Allah swears by the dawn, the pen, the fig, the soul.
aqsam-al-quran.l: The oath usually points at what follows it, so the thing sworn by is a clue to the truth being affirmed. The Prophet taught that people may swear only by Allah, and this is no contradiction: the Creator may swear by whatever He has made. Ibn al-Qayyim's at-Tibyan is the classic study of the subject.

ijaz-al-quran.s: The Qur'an's inimitability: that no one can produce its like, and the standing challenge to try.
ijaz-al-quran.l: The challenge is made in stages within the Qur'an, from producing ten surahs like it down to a single surah, addressed to the finest speakers of a language that prized poetry above everything. Classical scholars located the miracle mainly in the arrangement and cadence of the Arabic, not only in what is said. Modern claims about scientific miracles are a separate and much more contested argument.

tafsir.s: Explanation of the Qur'an: what a verse means, why it came, and what it asks of you.
tafsir.l: The word means to uncover, the way you pull a cover off a thing. A tafsir works through the text verse by verse using the rest of the Qur'an, the Sunnah, the sayings of the Companions and the Arabic language. Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi and al-Razi are among the best known, and they differ in focus, so reading one is not reading them all.

mufassir.s: A scholar who writes or teaches tafsir, trained in Arabic, the readings, the Sunnah and the occasions.
mufassir.l: Classical scholars set a demanding bar here, since an error is an error about the speech of Allah. The one thing a mufassir may never do is state what a verse means on the strength of personal opinion alone. Any reader may reflect on the Qur'an; explaining it authoritatively to others is a trained job.

tafsir-bil-mathur.s: Tafsir built on transmitted reports, as against tafsir bi'r-ra'y, which reasons from language and principle.
tafsir-bil-mathur.l: Transmitted tafsir explains the Qur'an by the Qur'an, then by the Sunnah, then by the Companions and their students. Reasoned tafsir uses grammar, context and legal principle; it is praised when it is disciplined and condemned when it is a person reading their preferences into the text. Most of the great commentaries mix the two rather than holding to one.

israiliyyat.s: Stories from earlier scriptures that entered tafsir to supply details the Qur'an deliberately leaves out.
israiliyyat.l: The Qur'an tells its stories for their lesson, so names, dates and numbers are often absent, and early commentators sometimes reached for Jewish and Christian material to fill the gaps. The rule scholars settled on has three parts: accept what our own sources confirm, reject what they contradict, and neither affirm nor deny the rest. A good deal of what people repeat as Qur'anic detail is actually israiliyyat.

tawil.s: Interpretation, and in a second sense the reality a statement finally turns out to refer to.
tawil.l: Early scholars used ta'wil and tafsir almost interchangeably; Tabari's great commentary carries the word in its title. Later it came to mean moving a word away from its apparent sense on the strength of evidence, which is where much theological argument lives. In Shia and Sufi writing the word often carries a further sense, an inner meaning beneath the plain one, which Sunni scholars accept only where it does not cancel the plain meaning.

tadabbur.s: Slow reflection on the Qur'an, letting a verse work on you instead of passing over it.
tadabbur.l: The root means to look at the far end of a thing, to follow it to its outcome. The Qur'an names this as the purpose of its revelation and asks more than once whether people reflect on it at all. Tadabbur is not tafsir: it needs no training, only attention, honesty, and enough of the meaning to know what you are reading.

tarjamah.s: A translation of the Qur'an, properly called a translation of the meanings rather than the Qur'an itself.
tarjamah.l: No translation carries the Arabic wording, and every translator has already made interpretive choices, so a translation is really a compressed tafsir. This is why prayer is recited in Arabic; Abu Hanifah is reported to have allowed reciting the meaning in prayer, his two main students allowed it only for someone genuinely unable, and he is reported to have come round to their view. A translated volume is also not given the same rulings as a mushaf.

tilawah.s: Reciting the Qur'an aloud, following its words closely rather than merely reading over them.
tilawah.l: The root carries the sense of following, one word behind another, which is why the term implies obedience as well as recitation. The Qur'an praises those who recite it as it deserves to be recited. In practice tilawah is done with wudu where possible, at a measured pace, opening with the isti'adhah.

tartil.s: Reciting slowly and distinctly, giving every letter its right, as the Qur'an itself instructs.
tartil.l: The command is direct: and recite the Qur'an with tartil. Ali is reported to have explained it as giving the letters their due and knowing where to stop. It was the Prophet's own pace, and it is the one to use if you want to understand what you are saying.

tadwir.s: The middle speed of recitation, sitting between the slow tartil and the quick hadr.
tadwir.l: It keeps every rule of tajwid fully in place while moving at a working pace. This is how most imams recite in tarawih and how most students revise. All three speeds are permitted; what is not permitted is speed that swallows letters.

hadr.s: Fast recitation that still keeps every rule intact, used mainly when revising memorisation.
hadr.l: Speed itself is allowed; dropping letters, cutting a madd short or blurring word endings is not. A hafiz revising several juz in a day will usually recite in hadr. If the words begin running into each other, the answer is to slow down rather than push on.

mujawwad.s: Two recorded styles: mujawwad is slow and ornamented for listening, murattal is even and plain.
mujawwad.l: Mujawwad is the style of the great reciters at public gatherings, with long pauses and phrases repeated at different pitches. Murattal moves steadily from beginning to end and is what most people use for daily listening and for memorising. Both must obey the same tajwid; the difference is delivery, not rules.

qari.s: A reciter of the Qur'an; in the classical sense, one trained and certified in a particular reading.
qari.l: The plural is qurra, and in the earliest generations it meant the scholars who carried the Qur'an rather than performers. A muqri is a qari licensed to teach and to grant ijazah. Today the word is used loosely for anyone who recites beautifully, which is harmless, but the older meaning is worth keeping in view.

tajwid.s: The rules for pronouncing the Qur'an correctly: each letter from its place, with its proper qualities.
tajwid.l: The word means to do a thing well. In practice it covers articulation points, letter qualities, lengthening, merging, hiding, and where to stop. Scholars broadly agree that learning enough to avoid errors that change meaning is required of every reciter; how much of the finer detail is obligatory is debated, and a beginner is not sinful for reciting imperfectly while learning.

makharij.s: The points in the mouth, throat and nose where each Arabic letter is produced.
makharij.l: Getting these right is what keeps letters apart, so that one throat letter does not slide into another, or sin into thaa. The most common count is seventeen points, grouped in the open air of the mouth, the throat, the tongue, the lips and the nose, though some early scholars counted sixteen or fourteen. They are learned out loud with a teacher, not from a diagram.

sifat-al-huruf.s: The qualities of each letter: whispered or voiced, heavy or light, tense or flowing.
sifat-al-huruf.l: Two letters can share one articulation point and still be different letters because their qualities differ, as with ta and da. Some qualities come in opposite pairs and some stand alone, like the whistle of sin or the roll of ra. Together with the makharij they are the two halves of pronouncing a letter correctly.

nun-sakinah.s: A nun carrying no vowel, or a tanwin ending, which triggers four tajwid rules depending on what follows.
nun-sakinah.l: Tanwin is the doubled vowel sign at the end of a word, sounded as an n. The letter that comes next decides what happens to it: izhar, idgham, iqlab or ikhfa. This single family of rules is where nearly every beginner's tajwid course starts.

izhar.s: Pronouncing a nun sakinah or tanwin clearly, with no nasal hum, before one of six throat letters.
izhar.l: The six are hamzah, ha, ayn, ha, ghayn and kha, all produced in the throat. Because the throat sits far from the nose, the nun is simply left as it is. There is a matching rule for a silent meem, called izhar shafawi, made at the lips.

idgham.s: Merging a nun sakinah or tanwin into the letter that follows, so the two are said as one.
idgham.l: The six letters are gathered in the word yarmaloon: ya, ra, meem, lam, waw and nun. With ya, nun, meem and waw the merge keeps a nasal hum; with lam and ra it does not. The term also covers any two identical or close letters running together, as when a word ending in dal meets a word beginning with dal.

iqlab.s: Turning a nun sakinah or tanwin into a meem when the next letter is ba, held with a hum.
iqlab.l: The lips come together lightly for the meem sound and the hum is held about two counts, without pressing the lips shut. Mushafs mark it with a small meem written above the nun or the tanwin. It happens with only one letter, ba, which makes it the easiest of the four rules to spot.

ikhfa.s: Hiding a nun sakinah or tanwin: not clear, not merged, held with a nasal hum for two counts.
ikhfa.l: It applies before fifteen letters, the ones left once the letters of izhar, idgham and iqlab are taken out. The tongue moves towards the position of the coming letter without quite touching, and the sound rests in the nose. There is a related lip rule, ikhfa shafawi, for a silent meem followed by ba.

ghunnah.s: The nasal hum carried by nun and meem, held about two counts wherever the rules require it.
ghunnah.l: It comes out through the nose, not the mouth: pinch your nose and the sound is cut off. It is fullest on a nun or meem carrying a shaddah, which is why those two are called the letters of ghunnah. It also appears inside idgham, ikhfa and iqlab.

qalqalah.s: The slight bounce on five letters when they carry no vowel: qaf, taa, ba, jim and dal.
qalqalah.l: Teachers gather them in the phrase qutbu jad. The bounce is small in the middle of a word and stronger when you stop on the letter at the end of a verse. It is a spring off the letter, not an added vowel, so no eh or uh sound should be heard after it.

madd.s: Lengthening a vowel with alif, waw or ya, held for a set number of counts.
madd.l: The natural madd is two counts and needs no sign in the text. Longer types are triggered by a hamzah or a sukun after the vowel and stretch to four, five or six counts depending on the type and the reading. Getting the count wrong can change a word entirely, which is why madd is drilled so hard.

tafkhim-tarqiq.s: Heavy and light pronunciation: some letters fill the mouth, others stay thin.
tafkhim-tarqiq.l: Seven letters are always heavy, gathered by teachers in a mnemonic phrase, khussa daghtin qiz. Ra and the lam in the name Allah switch between heavy and light depending on the vowels around them, and alif simply follows whatever came before it. The distinction is not decorative: a heavy letter said thin can turn one word into a different word.

imalah.s: Tilting a fatha towards a kasra, so the vowel lands somewhere between an a and an e.
imalah.l: It belongs to some readings far more than others; Warsh uses a lighter form of it, called taqlil, in many places. In the Hafs reading there is one clear case, in the word majreha in Surah Hud. It is a transmitted pronunciation, not a regional accent or a matter of taste.

waqf.s: Where you stop while reciting, and where you may not, shown by small letters above the line.
waqf.l: The familiar marks come from a system worked out by later scholars rather than from revelation: meem means stop, la means do not stop here, jeem means you may, and paired sets of three dots mean stop at one of the two but not both. Stopping in the wrong place can break the sense of a sentence, which is why the marks were added at all. The same word waqf also means a charitable endowment, an entirely separate subject.

saktah.s: A brief silence held without taking a breath, then the recitation carries straight on.
saktah.l: It keeps two words from running together in a way that could mislead the ear. In the Hafs reading there are four of them, in al-Kahf, Ya-Sin, al-Qiyamah and al-Mutaffifin, and the mushaf marks each with a small seen. Other readings place their pauses differently.

lahn.s: A mistake in recitation: the clear kind changes letters or vowels, the hidden kind breaks finer rules.
lahn.l: Lahn jali means mispronouncing a letter or a case ending, and because it can change the meaning, scholars treat correcting it as an obligation. Lahn khafi means shortening a madd, missing a ghunnah and the like, a matter of polish rather than sin. Everyone makes both while learning; the remedy is to recite to someone who can hear them.

hifz.s: Memorising the Qur'an by heart, traditionally with a teacher who hears you every day.
hifz.l: The word means preservation, the same word the Qur'an uses when it says Allah has taken the preservation of this revelation upon Himself. Memorisation has been the main way that happened: in every generation enough people carried the whole text that no copy could quietly go missing. A memoriser adds a small portion each day and spends far more time revising than adding.

hafiz-quran.s: Someone who has memorised the whole Qur'an and can recite it from memory.
hafiz-quran.l: The plural is huffaz and the feminine is hafizah. In the hadith sciences the same title means a scholar who has memorised a vast number of narrations, so it is not always about the Qur'an. It is not a permanent state either: without revision it slips away, which is why huffaz keep reciting for life.

murajaah.s: Revision of what you have memorised, the daily work that keeps the Qur'an from slipping away.
murajaah.l: The Prophet compared memorised Qur'an to tethered camels: let go of the rope and they are gone. Traditional schools split the day into new memorisation, recent revision and old revision, called sabaq, sabqi and manzil in South Asian madrasas. Most people who lose their hifz lose it here rather than in the memorising.

khatm.s: Completing a full reading of the Qur'an from beginning to end.
khatm.l: Many aim for one in Ramadan at a juz a day, and most mosques finish the whole text across the nights of tarawih. The Prophet told a Companion who wanted to read faster not to complete it in fewer than three days, because understanding suffers. The supplication read at the end is a widespread custom rather than a fixed text from the Sunnah.

sajdah-tilawah.s: The prostration made on reaching one of the Qur'an's marked verses of prostration, in prayer or outside it.
sajdah-tilawah.l: The mushaf marks these verses in the margin, usually with the word sajdah and a line above the text. The schools count them differently, at eleven, fourteen or fifteen, so mushafs printed in different regions mark a different number of them. It is a single prostration, and most scholars hold it is recommended rather than required, including for someone who is only listening.

mass-al-mushaf.s: Whether wudu is needed to hold a copy of the Qur'an; the four schools say yes, a minority disagrees.
mass-al-mushaf.l: The four Sunni schools require purity to touch the mushaf itself, citing a verse in Surah al-Waqi'ah and the Prophet's letter to the people of Yemen; Ibn Hazm and others read that verse as speaking about the angels instead. Reciting from memory without wudu is agreed to be fine. Most contemporary scholars hold that a phone or tablet is not a mushaf, so the ruling does not extend to reading from a screen.

sirah.s: The life story of the Prophet Muhammad, told in order, from birth to death.
sirah.l: The root means to travel, so a sirah is the road a person walked. The oldest surviving account is Ibn Ishaq's, preserved in the edition of Ibn Hisham, alongside al-Waqidi and the Tabaqat of Ibn Sa'd. Sirah writers accepted material on a looser standard of proof than the hadith scholars did, so a story being famous in the sirah does not by itself make it authentic.

sahabah.s: The Companions: anyone who met the Prophet as a believer and died still believing.
sahabah.l: The singular is sahabi. That definition is Ibn Hajar's, and it is deliberately wide, so a child lifted up to see him once counts alongside Abu Bakr. At the Farewell Pilgrimage the number present is traditionally given as more than a hundred thousand. Sunni scholarship holds them collectively upright in transmission, which is why hadith critics examine the chain from the generation after them onwards.

tabiun.s: The second generation: Muslims who met Companions but never met the Prophet himself.
tabiun.l: They are the ones who received Islam warm from the hands that had held it, and they built the first schools of law and Qur'an teaching. Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib, al-Hasan al-Basri, Ibn Sirin and Urwah ibn az-Zubayr belong here, and the Prophet named Uways al-Qarani the best of them without ever meeting him. The Prophet said the best of people are his generation, then those who follow them, then those who follow them.

tabi-al-tabiin.s: The third generation: those who met the Followers, the last age the Prophet praised by name.
tabi-al-tabiin.l: Malik ibn Anas, Sufyan ath-Thawri, al-Awza'i, Shu'bah and Abdullah ibn al-Mubarak stand in this layer. It is the generation in which the schools of law took shape and hadith began to be gathered into books rather than carried in memory alone. Together with the Companions and the Followers they make up the salaf, the three generations of praise.

salaf.s: The first three generations of Muslims: the Companions, the Followers, and those after them.
salaf.l: The word means those who went ahead, the way a caravan sends people forward. Ahl as-Sunnah treat their shared understanding as the safest reading of the Qur'an and Sunnah, on the reasoning that people closest to the source heard the language as it was meant. The modern movement label Salafi is a separate and contested usage; belonging to the salaf is a matter of century, not of party.

khulafa-rashidun.s: The four caliphs after the Prophet: Abu Bakr, Umar, Uthman and Ali.
khulafa-rashidun.l: Rashid means guided along a straight road. Their rule ran from the Prophet's death in the eleventh year of the Hijrah to the killing of Ali in the fortieth, close to thirty years. The Prophet told his community to hold to his sunnah and the sunnah of the rightly guided caliphs after him, which is why their practice carries a weight no later ruler's has. The title is Sunni usage; Shia hold that the succession belonged to Ali from the start. Some scholars add the six months of Hasan ibn Ali to complete the thirty years.

khilafah.s: Succession to the Prophet in governing the community, not in prophethood, which ended with him.
khilafah.l: The word means to come after someone and stand where they stood. The office ran through the Rashidun, the Umayyads, the Abbasids and finally the Ottoman claim, and was formally abolished in 1924. Worth knowing: when the Qur'an calls Adam a khalifah, and Dawud a khalifah on the earth, it means a steward answerable for what he is given, not the political office that later took the name.

ummah.s: The whole body of Muslims, across every land and century, treated as one community.
ummah.l: The root is umm, mother, so an ummah is a people gathered around one origin. The Qur'an calls this community a middle nation and says your ummah is one ummah, and it uses the same word for other nations, for a stretch of time, and once for Ibrahim alone, a single man called a whole community. In practice the word carries a duty: what happens to Muslims elsewhere is not other people's news.

hijrah.s: The Prophet's migration from Makkah to Madinah in 622, the start of the Muslim calendar.
hijrah.l: The word means to leave something behind and cut ties with it. He left with Abu Bakr, hid three nights in the cave of Thawr while Quraysh searched, and reached Madinah to build a mosque and a community that could finally live its faith openly. Umar later chose this event, not the Prophet's birth or the first revelation, as year one, because it was the moment the community became a community. The Prophet also said the true muhajir is the one who leaves what Allah forbade.

makkah.s: The valley city holding the Ka'bah, where the Prophet was born and revelation began.
makkah.l: The Qur'an also calls it Bakkah, and Umm al-Qura, the mother of settlements. Ibrahim left Hajar and Isma'il in it when it had no water and no people, and prayed that hearts would incline towards it. It is a haram, a sanctuary in which fighting, hunting and cutting the trees are forbidden. Most schools bar non Muslims from its precinct, the Hanafis being the exception, and the law in force there keeps them out of the city altogether. The Prophet lived there fifty three years before the Hijrah.

madinah.s: The oasis city that took the Prophet in, where he governed, died and is buried.
madinah.l: It was called Yathrib before he came; Madinat an-Nabi, the city of the Prophet, shortened to al-Madinah, the City. Its two Arab tribes, Aws and Khazraj, had been at war for generations and were reconciled by Islam. He declared it a sanctuary as Ibrahim had declared Makkah one, prayed for its measures to be blessed, and said that its hardship sifts people the way a furnace clears iron of impurity.

kabah.s: The stone cube at the centre of Makkah that Muslims face in every prayer.
kabah.l: The name comes from a word for a cube. The Qur'an describes Ibrahim and Isma'il raising its foundations, and calls it the first house appointed for mankind. Quraysh rebuilt it during the Prophet's youth and he settled their quarrel over who would set the Black Stone by carrying it on a cloak they all lifted together. Muslims face it, they do not worship it; it is a direction, and Umar said plainly of the Black Stone that it is a stone which neither harms nor benefits.

masjid-al-haram.s: The Sacred Mosque in Makkah, the enclosure built around the Ka'bah.
masjid-al-haram.l: Haram here means set apart and protected, not forbidden in the sense of sinful. It is the oldest of the three mosques a Muslim may set out on a journey to visit, and the Qur'an makes it the direction of prayer for everyone, wherever they are. A prayer offered in it is reported to be worth many times a prayer elsewhere. The open marble floor around the Ka'bah, where tawaf is made, is called the mataf.

masjid-an-nabawi.s: The Prophet's Mosque in Madinah, which he built himself and where he is buried.
masjid-an-nabawi.l: The first thing he did on arriving was buy the land and build it, with palm trunk pillars and a roof of fronds, and the poor Companions who had no home slept along its back wall. His own rooms opened onto it, and he was buried in Aishah's room, which later expansions brought inside the walls, under what is now the green dome. He said a prayer in it is better than a thousand prayers elsewhere, except in the Sacred Mosque.

masjid-al-aqsa.s: The mosque enclosure in Jerusalem, third of the three mosques worth travelling to visit.
masjid-al-aqsa.l: Aqsa means farthest, because it was the far end of the night journey from Makkah. It was the first qiblah, faced for roughly sixteen months before the direction turned to the Ka'bah. Common confusion worth clearing: al-Masjid al-Aqsa is the whole walled enclosure, including the golden Dome of the Rock and the silver domed prayer hall, not only the building people usually photograph.

rawdah.s: The space in the Prophet's Mosque between his house and his pulpit, called a garden of Paradise.
rawdah.l: The Prophet said that what lies between his house and his minbar is a garden from the gardens of Paradise. It is marked today by a green carpet where the rest of the mosque is red. Scholars read the saying two ways: that the ground itself is literally of Paradise, or that worship performed there leads to Paradise. Either way it is a place to pray in, not to touch, and crowding others out of it is not piety.

hijr-ismail.s: The low semicircular wall beside the Ka'bah, enclosing ground that is part of the original house.
hijr-ismail.l: When Quraysh rebuilt the Ka'bah they ran short of lawful money and left this stretch outside the walls. The Prophet told Aishah that if her people were not so new to Islam he would rebuild it on Ibrahim's foundation and bring the Hijr back inside. So praying in it counts as praying inside the Ka'bah, and this is also why tawaf must be made outside the wall, not between it and the building.

zamzam.s: The well beside the Ka'bah that opened for Hajar and her infant son Isma'il.
zamzam.l: Left in a dry valley with her baby, Hajar ran seven times between two hills looking for help, and water broke open at the child's feet. The name is said to come from her words as she banked the sand to hold it in. The well was lost for centuries and rediscovered by Abd al-Muttalib, the Prophet's grandfather. The Prophet said Zamzam water is for whatever it is drunk for, which is why people drink it with an intention rather than out of habit.

safa-marwah.s: Two small hills in Makkah, now enclosed in a corridor, walked between during hajj and umrah.
safa-marwah.l: The Qur'an names them among the symbols of Allah. Hajar crossed the ground between them seven times searching for water for Isma'il, and pilgrims repeat her crossing in the rite called sa'i. Both hills are now inside the Sacred Mosque, in a long marble gallery called the mas'a, and only the bare rock at each end still shows. It is a mother's desperate search preserved as an act of worship.

maqam-ibrahim.s: The stone Ibrahim stood on while building the Ka'bah, now under glass beside it.
maqam-ibrahim.l: The Qur'an commands that the station of Ibrahim be taken as a place of prayer, and pilgrims pray two units behind it after tawaf. The marks on the stone are traditionally described as the impressions of his feet. It is a landmark and a reminder, not a relic with power: it is not touched, kissed or wiped for blessing, and the two units are prayed towards the Ka'bah, not towards the stone.

jannat-al-baqi.s: The main cemetery of Madinah, where much of the Prophet's family and many Companions are buried.
jannat-al-baqi.l: The full name, Baqi al-Gharqad, refers to a thorn tree that once grew there. Uthman, Fatimah, Hasan ibn Ali, Aishah, Abbas and thousands of Companions lie in it. The Prophet used to visit at night and greet its people. Its graves are left level and unmarked, on his instruction that graves be kept low and not built over. The domes that later centuries raised over them were demolished in 1926, a decision Muslims still argue over, so visitors find open ground rather than monuments.

jahiliyyah.s: The age of ignorance in Arabia before Islam, and any conduct that still belongs to it.
jahiliyyah.l: The root is jahl, which means recklessness and hot headed ignorance rather than illiteracy. The Arabs of that age had poetry, memory, hospitality and law, so the word is a verdict on their worship and their violence, not on their intelligence. It also names a condition rather than only a period: the Prophet told Abu Dharr, after he insulted a man over his mother, that he was a man with jahiliyyah still in him.

am-al-fil.s: The year an army with an elephant marched on the Ka'bah and was destroyed, around 570.
am-al-fil.l: Abrahah, ruling Yemen, came to pull the Ka'bah down so pilgrims would come to his own church instead. Surah al-Fil describes birds pelting the army with stones of baked clay until they were left like chewed straw. The Prophet was born in that year or close to it, and Arabs dated events from it for a generation afterwards. Abd al-Muttalib's answer to Abrahah is famous: the House has a Lord who will protect it.

ghar-hira.s: The small cave above Makkah where the Prophet was praying when revelation first came.
ghar-hira.l: It sits near the top of Jabal an-Nur, the mountain of light, a hard climb even now. He used to withdraw there for nights at a time before prophethood, and it was there that Jibril pressed him and said Read. He came home shaking and asked to be covered, and Khadijah wrapped him and told him Allah would never disgrace him. He is not reported to have returned to the cave afterwards, so climbing it is a matter of history, not a rite.

shib-abi-talib.s: The Makkan valley where the Prophet's clan was penned by a boycott for about three years.
shib-abi-talib.l: Quraysh hung a written pact in the Ka'bah agreeing to no trade and no marriage with Banu Hashim until they surrendered him. Believer and unbeliever of the clan were shut in together, living on what sympathisers smuggled past the guards, and children's crying could be heard outside. It broke when several Quraysh who had never been comfortable with it tore the document up. Khadijah and Abu Talib both died soon after, in what is called the Year of Sorrow.

hijrah-habashah.s: The first migration, when persecuted Muslims fled Makkah to a Christian king in Abyssinia.
hijrah-habashah.l: It happened in two waves, years before the move to Madinah. The Prophet sent them to the Negus, whom he described as a king under whom nobody is wronged. Quraysh sent envoys with gifts to demand them back; Ja'far ibn Abi Talib answered by describing what they had been and what Islam made of them, then recited from Surah Maryam, and the king wept and refused to hand them over. Some stayed until after Khaybar.

isra-miraj.s: The night the Prophet was taken to Jerusalem and then raised through the heavens.
isra-miraj.l: Isra is the journey by night to al-Masjid al-Aqsa, where he led the prophets in prayer; mi'raj is the ascent from there. The Qur'an opens Surah al-Isra with the journey and Surah an-Najm describes what he saw at the Lote Tree. It was on this night that the five daily prayers were given, reduced from fifty at Musa's urging. Sunni scholars overwhelmingly hold it was in body and not only in vision, and the exact date is not established.

bayat-al-aqabah.s: Two secret pledges by men of Madinah that opened the way for the Hijrah.
bayat-al-aqabah.l: They were made at a mountain pass near Mina during the pilgrimage season. In the first, twelve men promised to worship none but Allah and to keep away from theft, adultery, infanticide and slander, and Mus'ab ibn Umayr was sent back with them as teacher. A year later roughly seventy men and two women pledged to protect him as they would protect their own families, knowing exactly what it would cost. Within months the Muslims of Makkah began slipping away to Madinah.

ghar-thawr.s: The cave south of Makkah where the Prophet and Abu Bakr hid three nights during the Hijrah.
ghar-thawr.l: Quraysh had put a price on his head and search parties came close enough for Abu Bakr to see their feet. The Qur'an records the moment in Surah at-Tawbah, calling him the second of two when they were in the cave, and quoting his words to his companion: do not grieve, Allah is with us. The verse is the strongest single proof Sunnis cite for Abu Bakr's rank. Abu Bakr was in his fifties and climbed the mountain in the dark.

sahifat-al-madinah.s: The written charter the Prophet drew up on reaching Madinah, binding its tribes into one body.
sahifat-al-madinah.l: It made the Muhajirun and Ansar and the Jewish tribes of the city into a single political community for defence, fixed responsibility for blood money clan by clan, and stated that the Jews had their religion and the Muslims theirs. Disputes were to be referred to the Prophet. Its text is preserved in the sirah literature rather than in the hadith collections, and historians treat it as among the earliest documents of the Muslim community.

ghazwah.s: A military expedition the Prophet led in person, as opposed to one he sent out under another.
ghazwah.l: An expedition he dispatched without going himself is a sariyyah. Historians count the ghazawat in the twenties and the sariyyah in the dozens, though the lists differ, and in most of them no fighting actually occurred. The genre of books recording them is called maghazi, and it is the oldest layer of sirah writing. The word by itself means a raid; it carries no ruling, and it is not a synonym for jihad.

badr.s: The first major battle, in year two, where about three hundred Muslims defeated a much larger force.
badr.l: It began as an attempt to intercept a caravan and became a pitched fight against roughly a thousand Quraysh. The Qur'an calls the day the Furqan, the day of separation, and describes angels sent to support the believers. Fathers faced sons and brothers faced brothers in it. Those who fought at Badr, the Badriyyun, hold a rank of their own; the Prophet indicated that Allah had looked upon them and forgiven them.

uhud.s: The battle at the mountain outside Madinah where an early Muslim advantage collapsed into losses.
uhud.l: The Prophet posted archers on a hill and told them not to leave it whatever happened. When Quraysh broke and the Muslims began collecting spoils, most of the archers came down, and Khalid ibn al-Walid's cavalry came round the open flank. Around seventy Companions were killed, including Hamzah, and the Prophet himself was wounded. Surah Al Imran discusses the day at length, without softening it, which is part of why the Qur'an's honesty about its own community is striking.

khandaq.s: The siege of Madinah in year five, met by digging a trench across the city's open side.
khandaq.l: A confederacy of Quraysh and allied tribes came to finish the matter, outnumbering the defenders several times over. Salman al-Farisi suggested the Persian tactic of a trench, which the Arabs had not seen, and the Muslims dug it in bitter cold and hunger with stones tied against their stomachs. After weeks of siege a winter wind tore the camp apart and the confederacy went home. Surah al-Ahzab is named for them and describes the fear of that month plainly.

hudaybiyah.s: The treaty of year six that looked like a defeat and opened the way to the conquest of Makkah.
hudaybiyah.l: The Prophet set out for umrah and was stopped short of Makkah. The terms felt humiliating: go home this year, ten years of truce, and hand back anyone who comes to you from Quraysh, and Umar objected openly. Under a tree there the Companions pledged not to flee, the pledge the Qur'an calls Ridwan, and Surah al-Fath then called the treaty a clear victory. Peace let people hear the Qur'an without a war between them, and more entered Islam in those two years than in the nineteen before.

khaybar.s: The fortified oasis north of Madinah taken in year seven, shortly after Hudaybiyah.
khaybar.l: Its forts had become the base from which the confederacy against Madinah was organised. The Prophet gave the banner to Ali after saying he would give it to a man who loves Allah and His Messenger and is loved by them. After the surrender the land was left with its farmers on a share of the harvest, an arrangement later cited in the law of crop sharing. It was here that Ja'far returned from Abyssinia, and the Prophet said he did not know which gladdened him more.

ghazwat-mutah.s: The first clash with Byzantine forces, in year eight, where three appointed commanders fell in turn.
ghazwat-mutah.l: The Prophet named Zayd ibn Harithah to lead, then Ja'far ibn Abi Talib if Zayd fell, then Abdullah ibn Rawahah if Ja'far fell. All three were killed. Khalid ibn al-Walid, newly Muslim, took up the banner and extracted the army intact, and the Prophet called him a sword among the swords of Allah. He is reported to have described the deaths to the Companions in Madinah while the battle was still being fought far away. He did not go himself, so by the strict usage it is a sariyyah rather than a ghazwah.

fath-makkah.s: The Prophet's return to Makkah in year eight, taken almost without a fight.
fath-makkah.l: Quraysh had broken the Hudaybiyah truce, and he came with an army large enough to make resistance pointless. He entered with his head bowed low over his mount, cleared the idols from around the Ka'bah, and told the people who had driven him out and killed his family that they could go, there was no blame on them today. Surah an-Nasr, about people entering the religion in crowds, belongs to this moment. He also declared that there is no hijrah after the conquest.

hunayn.s: The ambush weeks after the conquest of Makkah, where confidence in numbers nearly cost the battle.
hunayn.l: Twelve thousand Muslims marched out against Hawazin and Thaqif, and some said openly that they would not be beaten today for smallness of number. Archers hidden in the narrow valley broke the front and most of the army turned; a small group stood with the Prophet until the line re formed. Surah at-Tawbah names Hunayn and says their numbers pleased them but availed them nothing. The captured wealth was distributed in a way that tested the Ansar, and his answer to them made them weep.

tabuk.s: The last expedition the Prophet led, a long march north in year nine that ended without battle.
tabuk.l: It was called the army of hardship: high summer, scarce water, ripe harvests left behind, and a distant enemy. Uthman equipped a large part of it from his own wealth. No fighting took place. Its lasting story is the three Companions who simply failed to go and would not lie about why; the community was told to shun them for fifty nights until Surah at-Tawbah announced that Allah had turned to them, a passage that is really about honesty when a lie would have been easy.

hajjat-al-wada.s: The only hajj the Prophet performed after it was made obligatory, in year ten.
hajjat-al-wada.l: More than a hundred thousand people came, and he told them to take their rites from him, which is why almost every detail of the hajj is traced to those days. He stood at Arafah and delivered the farewell sermon there. The verse saying the religion has been completed was revealed on that afternoon; when a Jewish man later remarked that such a verse would have been a festival for his people, Umar replied that it came on a day that was already two festivals.

khutbat-al-wada.s: The sermon given at Arafah during the Farewell Pilgrimage, months before the Prophet died.
khutbat-al-wada.l: The reports of it are scattered across several narrations rather than one continuous text, and popular printed versions blend them. What is firmly established: he declared blood, property and honour sacred among Muslims as sacred as that day and that place; he cancelled the interest and blood feuds of jahiliyyah, beginning with his own family's claims; he charged the men to fear Allah regarding women; and he said he was leaving them what they would not go astray by holding to. He asked them three times whether he had delivered the message.

ansar.s: The Muslims of Madinah who took in the emigrants from Makkah and shared everything with them.
ansar.l: The word means the helpers. They were the two tribes of Aws and Khazraj, long at war until Islam reconciled them. The Prophet paired each emigrant with a host in a formal bond of brotherhood, and the Qur'an says they preferred others over themselves even while in need. He told them that love of the Ansar is a mark of faith and dislike of them a mark of hypocrisy, and he died and was buried among them.

muhajirun.s: The Muslims who left Makkah for Madinah, leaving homes and property behind.
muhajirun.l: The singular is muhajir, one who cuts ties and moves. They arrived with nothing and the Qur'an praises them alongside the Ansar as the first and foremost. Emigration from Makkah specifically ended with the conquest, when the Prophet said there is no hijrah after the opening, but striving and intention remain. He also defined the muhajir in a wider sense: the one who abandons what Allah has forbidden.

ahl-al-bayt.s: The Prophet's household, honoured by all Muslims, though the schools draw its boundary differently.
ahl-al-bayt.l: The verse of purification in Surah al-Ahzab sits in a passage addressing his wives, and a hadith records him gathering Ali, Fatimah, Hasan and Husayn under a cloak and praying for them. Most Sunni scholars therefore include both the wives and that close family, and many add the wider clan of Banu Hashim who are forbidden to take zakat. Twelver Shia restrict the term to the five of the cloak and the Imams descended from them. Loving them is agreed; the boundary is not.

ummahat-al-muminin.s: The Prophet's wives, whom the Qur'an names as mothers to every believer.
ummahat-al-muminin.l: Surah al-Ahzab says his wives are their mothers, and in the same surah forbids anyone to marry them after him. He was married to eleven women across his life, nine of whom survived him; for twenty five years, until he was fifty, he was married to Khadijah alone. Several were widows, and the marriages knitted together tribes that had been enemies. Aishah and Umm Salamah in particular transmitted a large part of what is known about his private practice.

asharah-mubashsharah.s: Ten Companions named together in one narration as promised Paradise while still alive.
asharah-mubashsharah.l: They are Abu Bakr, Umar, Uthman, Ali, Talhah, az-Zubayr, Abd ar-Rahman ibn Awf, Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, Sa'id ibn Zayd and Abu Ubaydah ibn al-Jarrah. The point is not that only ten were promised Paradise; others, including Khadijah, Fatimah, Bilal and the people of Badr, were given similar news in separate reports. These ten are simply the ones listed in a single hadith, which is why they are remembered as a set.

khadijah.s: The Prophet's first wife and the first person of all to believe in him.
khadijah.l: She was a merchant of standing in Makkah who hired him for his honesty and then proposed marriage. When he came down from Hira shaking, she covered him and said Allah would never disgrace a man who carries the weak and gives to the destitute. She spent her wealth on the boycott years and died in the Year of Sorrow, before the Hijrah. All his children except Ibrahim were hers, and Jibril once sent her greetings of peace and news of a house in Paradise.

aishah.s: The Prophet's wife, daughter of Abu Bakr, and one of the greatest scholars among the Companions.
aishah.l: She narrated over two thousand hadith, much of it about his life at home, and senior Companions came to her with questions of law and inheritance. When she was accused of adultery by rumour, the community was left in suspense for about a month before verses in Surah an-Nur cleared her and set the rule that such a charge needs four witnesses. She later took a side in the first civil war and afterwards spoke of it with open regret. She died in Madinah and is buried in al-Baqi.

fatimah.s: The Prophet's youngest daughter, wife of Ali and mother of Hasan and Husayn.
fatimah.l: She lived plainly; the famous exchange in which she asked her father for a servant and was taught words of remembrance instead is well known. He said she was a part of him, and that whoever angers her angers him. In his final illness he whispered something that made her weep and then something that made her smile: that he was dying, and that she would be the first of his household to follow him. She died about six months later, in her twenties.

abu-bakr.s: The Prophet's closest friend, his companion in the cave, and the first caliph.
abu-bakr.l: He is called as-Siddiq, the one who confirms, for believing the night journey without hesitation when others scoffed. He freed Bilal and other tortured slaves with his own money, and the Prophet appointed him to lead the prayer in his final illness. His caliphate lasted about two years and was mostly spent holding the community together through the wars of apostasy; he also ordered the Qur'an gathered into a single written copy. He is buried beside the Prophet.

umar-ibn-al-khattab.s: The second caliph, called al-Faruq, under whom the Muslim state expanded enormously.
umar-ibn-al-khattab.l: He had set out to kill the Prophet and accepted Islam on the road, after hearing Surah Ta Ha in his sister's house. As caliph for about ten years he took Syria, Egypt, Iraq and Persia, and built the machinery of a state: a treasury, a stipend register, provincial governors held to account, and the Hijri calendar. Several rulings were revealed in line with opinions he had voiced. He walked Madinah at night without guards, and was stabbed while leading fajr.

uthman-ibn-affan.s: The third caliph, called Dhun-Nurayn, who fixed the Qur'an in one agreed written text.
uthman-ibn-affan.l: The title means possessor of two lights, because he married two of the Prophet's daughters in turn. He was wealthy and gave heavily: he bought the well of Rumah for the people of Madinah and equipped much of the army of Tabuk. His great act as caliph was to standardise the mushaf, sending official copies to the provinces when he saw reciters disputing over readings. Rebels besieged his house and killed him while he was reading the Qur'an; he refused to let anyone fight for him.

ali-ibn-abi-talib.s: The Prophet's cousin and son in law, raised by him, and the fourth caliph.
ali-ibn-abi-talib.l: He was the first child to accept Islam and slept in the Prophet's bed on the night of the Hijrah so the assassins would think he was still there. He married Fatimah, carried the banner at Khaybar, and was known for both learning and courage. His caliphate, from the thirty fifth to the fortieth year, was consumed by the first civil war; he moved the capital to Kufa and was killed in its mosque. Sunnis count him the fourth of the rightly guided caliphs; Shia hold him to be the first Imam and the rightful successor from the start.

hamzah.s: The Prophet's uncle, called the Lion of Allah, killed at Uhud.
hamzah.l: He accepted Islam in anger, hearing that Abu Jahl had abused his nephew, and his conversion changed the balance of pressure on the Muslims in Makkah. He fought at Badr and was killed at Uhud by Wahshi, a man promised his freedom for the deed, and the Prophet was profoundly grieved by the state of his body. Years later Wahshi accepted Islam and was forgiven, though the Prophet asked him to keep his face out of sight. Hamzah is remembered as the chief of the martyrs.

bilal.s: An enslaved Abyssinian tortured for his faith, freed by Abu Bakr, and the first to call the adhan.
bilal.l: His owner pinned him under a rock in the midday heat of Makkah and he answered only with one word, ahad, one. Abu Bakr bought him and set him free. When the Muslims settled in Madinah and needed a way to gather people, he was given the call to prayer, and on the day Makkah was taken he climbed onto the Ka'bah to make it. The Prophet told him he had heard his footsteps ahead of him in Paradise, and Bilal explained he prayed after every wudu.

musab-ibn-umayr.s: The best dressed youth in Makkah who gave it up, taught Madinah Islam, and died at Uhud.
musab-ibn-umayr.l: His mother had raised him in luxury and cut him off when he believed. After the first pledge at Aqabah the Prophet sent him alone to Madinah as teacher and reciter, and through him whole households of the Aws and Khazraj entered Islam before the Hijrah. He carried the banner at Uhud and was killed there. When they came to bury him they had only one short cloak: covering his head left his feet bare, and covering his feet left his head bare.

khalid-ibn-al-walid.s: The commander called the Sword of Allah, who fought against the Muslims before joining them.
khalid-ibn-al-walid.l: His cavalry turned the day against the Muslims at Uhud. He accepted Islam before the conquest of Makkah, saved the army at Mu'tah, and then led the campaigns against the false prophets and into Syria, where Yarmuk broke Byzantine power in the region. Umar removed him from command while he was winning, reportedly so people would learn that victory comes from Allah and not from a man. He accepted it and served under his replacement, and died in his bed in Homs.

salman-al-farisi.s: A Persian who searched through two religions for the truth and was enslaved before finding it.
salman-al-farisi.l: He left his father's fire worship for Christianity, served a succession of monks, and was told by the last of them that a prophet was about to appear in a land of date palms. On the way he was betrayed and sold as a slave into Madinah, where he recognised the signs he had been described. The Companions helped him buy his freedom. At the Trench it was his suggestion, unknown to the Arabs, that saved the city, and the Prophet is reported to have said Salman is of us, the people of the house.

abu-hurayrah.s: The Companion who narrated more hadith than any other, from about four years in the Prophet's company.
abu-hurayrah.l: The nickname means father of the kitten, from a cat he carried as a boy. He accepted Islam around the year of Khaybar, joined the poor Companions living on the mosque bench, and stayed close to the Prophet while others worked or traded. He said openly that the Muhajirun were busy in the markets and the Ansar with their land, and he was not. He also asked the Prophet to pray that he would not forget, and reported that he never forgot anything afterwards.

hasan-ibn-ali.s: The Prophet's elder grandson, who gave up the caliphate to stop a war between Muslims.
hasan-ibn-ali.l: After Ali was killed the people of Iraq pledged to him, and Mu'awiyah held Syria. Rather than fight, he negotiated terms and stepped aside in the forty first year, and that year is called the Year of Unity. The Prophet had said of him, while he was a child on the pulpit, that this son of his is a master and that Allah would reconcile two great parties of Muslims through him. Twelver Shia count him the second Imam, and he is buried in al-Baqi.

husayn-ibn-ali.s: The Prophet's younger grandson, killed at Karbala in the sixty first year of the Hijrah.
husayn-ibn-ali.l: When Mu'awiyah died and rule passed to his son Yazid, Husayn refused to pledge allegiance and set out for Kufa on the invitation of its people. They abandoned him, and he was surrounded at Karbala with a small band of family and followers, cut off from water, and killed with most of the men of his household. The Prophet had said that he and Hasan were the masters of the youth of Paradise. His death remains one of the deepest wounds in Muslim memory.

hurub-al-riddah.s: Abu Bakr's campaigns against tribes that broke away after the Prophet died.
hurub-al-riddah.l: Some tribes rejected Islam outright, some followed men claiming prophethood such as Musaylimah, and some kept the prayer but refused to pay zakat to Madinah. Abu Bakr insisted on all of it, saying he would fight anyone who separated what the Prophet had joined, and Umar, who had hesitated, came to agree. The heaviest battle was Yamamah, where so many memorisers of the Qur'an were killed that Umar urged Abu Bakr to have it collected in one written copy.

al-fitnah-al-ula.s: The first civil war among Muslims, from the killing of Uthman to the death of Ali.
al-fitnah-al-ula.l: Fitnah means a fire that tests metal, and then any trial that separates people. It ran from the thirty fifth to the fortieth year of the Hijrah: the murder of Uthman, the Battle of the Camel, Siffin, the failed arbitration, and the breaking away of the Kharijites who then killed Ali. Sunni scholarship holds that both sides were Companions acting on interpretation, that Ali was closer to the truth, and that the settled adab is to restrain the tongue about what happened.

karbala.s: The plain in Iraq where Husayn and his household were killed on the tenth of Muharram, year 61.
karbala.l: He had refused to pledge to Yazid and was travelling to Kufa when the army sent to intercept him cut him off from the Euphrates. Around seventy of his party were killed, including his family, and the survivors were taken to Damascus. Sunnis regard it as a grievous crime and grieve it without ritual observance, while Twelver Shia commemorate it every Muharram as a central act of devotion. Whatever a Muslim's school, the grandson of the Prophet was killed by people who called themselves Muslims.

banu-umayyah.s: The first dynasty of caliphs, ruling from Damascus for about ninety years after the Rashidun.
banu-umayyah.l: It began with Mu'awiyah ibn Abi Sufyan, a Companion and scribe of revelation, and turned the caliphate into an inherited office. Under them the state reached Spain in the west and the Indus in the east, Arabic became the language of administration, coinage was reformed, and the Dome of the Rock was built. Muslim assessment of them is mixed and always has been. Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz, the exception nearly everyone praises, came from this family.

umar-ibn-abd-al-aziz.s: The Umayyad caliph whose short reign is remembered as a return to the way of the Rashidun.
umar-ibn-abd-al-aziz.l: He ruled about two and a half years from the ninety ninth year of the Hijrah. He returned property his family had taken, stopped the cursing of Ali from the pulpits, lightened taxes on new Muslims, and lived so plainly that his own household noticed the change first. He is also the caliph who ordered hadith to be gathered and written down systematically, which is why so much survives. Many scholars call him the fifth of the rightly guided caliphs.

abu-hanifah.s: The earliest of the four imams, a Kufan merchant whose school is the most widely followed today.
abu-hanifah.l: He was born around the year 80 and died in 150, in Baghdad. He is often counted among the Tabi'un on the basis that he may have seen the Companion Anas ibn Malik as a child, though scholars discuss this. He taught by argument in a circle rather than by dictation, and his students Abu Yusuf and Muhammad ash-Shaybani wrote the school down. He refused the post of chief judge and died in prison, and he is remembered as much for that refusal as for his law.

imam-malik.s: The imam of Madinah, who taught in the Prophet's mosque and wrote the Muwatta.
imam-malik.l: He died in 179 and spent almost his whole life in the city, on the reasoning that its inherited practice was itself a form of evidence. The Muwatta is among the earliest surviving books to put hadith and legal rulings side by side. He was flogged for a ruling that displeased the authorities and did not retract it. When a caliph proposed making his book the single law of the empire he refused, saying the Companions had scattered and people had learned different things.

imam-al-shafii.s: The imam who wrote the first book on how law is derived, bridging Madinah and Iraq.
imam-al-shafii.l: Born in Gaza in 150 and died in Egypt in 204, of the Prophet's wider clan. He memorised the Muwatta and studied with Malik in Madinah, then with Abu Hanifah's student ash-Shaybani in Iraq, and so held both approaches in one head. His Risalah set out the sources of law in order and is the foundation of usul al-fiqh as a discipline. He revised his own positions after moving to Egypt, which is why the school records an old and a new opinion on some questions.

imam-ahmad.s: The imam of hadith who was flogged rather than say the Qur'an was created.
imam-ahmad.l: He died in 241 in Baghdad. His Musnad gathers tens of thousands of reports arranged by the Companion who narrated them rather than by subject. Under three caliphs he was put to the test over the doctrine that the Qur'an is created, imprisoned and beaten, and refused; when the policy was finally reversed his stand was seen as having held the community's creed steady. He is reported to have forgiven the man who flogged him, and he resisted having his opinions written down as a school at all.

imam-al-bukhari.s: The scholar from Bukhara who compiled the Sahih, the most rigorously sifted book of hadith.
imam-al-bukhari.l: Born in 194, he lost his sight as a child and had it restored, and began memorising hadith before he was ten. He travelled for years across the Muslim world collecting reports, and required proof that a narrator had actually met the person he quoted, a stricter condition than most. Beyond the Sahih he wrote al-Adab al-Mufrad on manners and at-Tarikh al-Kabir on narrators. He died in exile near Samarqand in 256, after a dispute over a theological question.

imam-muslim.s: The compiler of the second Sahih, a student and close friend of al-Bukhari.
imam-muslim.l: He was from Nishapur and died in 261, a few years after his teacher. He held that two narrators living in the same period with the possibility of meeting is enough, without proof of an actual meeting, which is the main methodological difference between the two books. He gathered every chain of a hadith in one place instead of scattering them, which makes his book easier to study. His introduction is a short treatise on hadith criticism and is still read on its own.

hijri-calendar.s: The Muslim lunar calendar, counting years from the Hijrah and running about eleven days shorter than the solar year.
hijri-calendar.l: Umar established it, choosing the Hijrah as year one rather than the Prophet's birth or the first revelation. Its twelve months are Muharram, Safar, Rabi al-Awwal, Rabi ath-Thani, Jumada al-Ula, Jumada al-Akhirah, Rajab, Sha'ban, Ramadan, Shawwal, Dhul Qa'dah and Dhul Hijjah, and four of them are sacred. Because it is purely lunar, Ramadan and hajj move through all the seasons over roughly thirty three years, so every generation fasts both the long days and the short ones.

ashura.s: The tenth of Muharram, a day the Prophet fasted for the deliverance of Musa from Pharaoh.
ashura.l: Arriving in Madinah he found the Jews fasting it and said that he had more right to Musa than they did. Fasting it is recommended and is reported to expiate the previous year; he intended to add the ninth as well, so most fast both. It is also the day Husayn was killed at Karbala in the sixty first year. Sunnis do not treat it as a day of mourning ritual, while Twelver Shia observe it as the central commemoration of that loss.

tazkiyah.s: The purification of the self: the work of clearing the heart of what spoils it.
tazkiyah.l: The Qur'an says the one who purifies the soul has succeeded (Qur'an 91:9), and lists purifying people among the tasks the Prophet peace be upon him was sent with (Qur'an 62:2). The subject covers both halves of the job: removing what is blameworthy, such as envy and arrogance, and planting what is praiseworthy, such as sincerity and gratitude. It is a discipline with a syllabus, not a mood, and it belongs to every Muslim rather than to one group.

qalb.s: The heart: in the Qur'an the seat of understanding and intention, not the organ alone.
qalb.l: The Qur'an speaks of a sound heart brought to Allah (Qur'an 26:89), of hearts that are sealed, and of hearts covered by rust from what they earned (Qur'an 83:14). The Prophet peace be upon him said there is a morsel of flesh in the body which, if it is sound, makes the whole body sound, and it is the heart, in Bukhari and Muslim. Classical writers describe it in three states: sound, sick, and dead. This is why the science of the heart is treated as a discipline and not a mood.

taqwa.s: An alert, careful awareness of Allah that keeps a person away from what harms them.
taqwa.l: The root means to guard or to shield, and carries the sense of putting something between yourself and danger. The Qur'an calls it the best provision for the journey (Qur'an 2:197), and the Prophet peace be upon him pointed to his chest three times and said taqwa is here, in a report collected by Muslim. It is not fear alone, and it is not a personality type. It is caution kept awake.

ikhlas.s: Doing an act for Allah alone, with no eye on who else is watching.
ikhlas.l: The word means to make something pure, with nothing mixed into it. The Qur'an says people were commanded only to worship Allah, sincerely devoting religion to Him (Qur'an 98:5), and the Prophet peace be upon him said actions are only by intentions, in Bukhari and Muslim. Ikhlas is not a feeling you generate before an act. It is what is left of the act when the praise does not arrive.

riya.s: Performing worship so that people will see it, which empties the act of its reward.
riya.l: The word comes from seeing, and its close cousin sum'ah is doing something so that people will hear of it. The Qur'an condemns those who pray only to be seen (Qur'an 107:6), and the Prophet peace be upon him called showing off the lesser shirk, in a report from Imam Ahmad. Being pleased that someone noticed a good deed is not riya. Riya is when being noticed was the reason you did it.

sidq.s: Truthfulness: that your words, your intentions and your actions all report the same thing.
sidq.l: The Qur'an tells the believers to be with the truthful (Qur'an 9:119), and the Prophet peace be upon him said truthfulness leads to righteousness and righteousness leads to Paradise, in Bukhari and Muslim. Writers on the heart use sidq more widely than honest speech: a truthful hope, a truthful repentance, a truthful claim to love Allah. In that sense its opposite is not only lying but posing.

sabr.s: Holding yourself steady under what is hard, without complaint to creation and without giving up.
sabr.l: The root means to restrain or to confine. Scholars usually give it three fields: steadiness in obeying Allah, steadiness in staying away from what He forbade, and steadiness under what He decrees. The Qur'an pairs it with prayer as the two things to seek help by (Qur'an 2:153). It does not mean feeling nothing: the Prophet peace be upon him wept when his son died and said the eye weeps and the heart grieves, but we say only what pleases our Lord, in Bukhari.

shukr.s: Gratitude that shows: knowing the gift, saying so, and using it as its Giver would like.
shukr.l: The Qur'an promises increase to those who are grateful (Qur'an 14:7). Scholars describe shukr working in three places at once: the heart admits where the gift came from, the tongue says it, and the limbs do not use the gift against the One who gave it. The Prophet peace be upon him also said that whoever does not thank people has not thanked Allah, in Abu Dawud and Tirmidhi.

tawakkul.s: Relying on Allah for the outcome while still doing the work that leads to it.
tawakkul.l: The Qur'an says whoever relies on Allah, He is enough for him (Qur'an 65:3), and it also tells the Prophet peace be upon him to consult, then decide, then rely (Qur'an 3:159). When a man asked whether to leave his camel loose and trust Allah, he was told to tie it and then trust, in a report collected by Tirmidhi. Tawakkul is the state of the heart after you have done what you can, not a reason to do nothing.

rida.s: Contentment with what Allah decrees, so the heart stops arguing with what already happened.
rida.l: The word means to be pleased, and it runs both ways: Allah pleased with the believer and the believer pleased with Him (Qur'an 98:8). Scholars distinguish it from sabr, which holds steady under a blow, while rida no longer wishes the blow away. It applies to what has already been decreed. It does not mean accepting oppression, and it does not stop anyone from seeking a remedy.

khawf.s: Fear of Allah: the awareness of His justice that keeps a person from walking off the edge.
khawf.l: The Qur'an describes believers as those whose hearts tremble when Allah is mentioned (Qur'an 8:2), and as calling on their Lord in fear and hope together (Qur'an 32:16). Scholars say the two wings must stay even: fear alone tips into despair, hope alone tips into carelessness. Healthy khawf is measured by what it makes you do, not by how bad it makes you feel.

raja.s: Hope in Allah's mercy, held by someone who is still working, not by someone who has stopped.
raja.l: The Qur'an forbids despair of Allah's mercy and says He forgives all sins (Qur'an 39:53). Scholars separate raja' from wishful thinking, tamanni: hope plants and then expects a crop, wishing expects a crop with no seed. A common counsel is to keep fear slightly ahead while a person is in health, and to keep hope ahead when death is near.

mahabbah.s: Love of Allah, measured less by what it feels like and more by what it follows.
mahabbah.l: The Qur'an says those who believe are strongest in love of Allah (Qur'an 2:165), and gives the test plainly: if you love Allah, follow the Messenger, and Allah will love you (Qur'an 3:31). Its signs are usually listed as preferring what He loves over what you want, ease in remembering Him, and love for the people who love Him. Sufi writers dwell on this station at length, but it is not a Sufi invention. It is in the verse.

khushu-al-qalb.s: The heart's stillness and lowering before Allah, of which focus in prayer is one part.
khushu-al-qalb.l: The Qur'an asks whether the time has not come for the hearts of the believers to soften at the remembrance of Allah (Qur'an 57:16), which is khushu' outside the prayer as well as inside it. It is closer to a lowering than to an emotion: the heart stops standing up straight in front of its Lord. For khushu' specifically during salah, see the separate entry under worship.

dhikr.s: Remembrance of Allah, in set phrases and in the wider habit of not forgetting Him.
dhikr.l: The Qur'an says hearts find rest in the remembrance of Allah (Qur'an 13:28) and tells believers to remember Him and He will remember them (Qur'an 2:152). In practice dhikr covers the short phrases such as subhan Allah and la ilaha illa Allah, the morning and evening adhkar, reciting the Qur'an, and the wider state of living aware of Him. Sufi orders add group and audible forms, and that is where scholars disagree about method, not about dhikr itself.

dua.s: Asking Allah directly, in any language, at any time, for anything permitted.
dua.l: The Qur'an says call on Me and I will answer you (Qur'an 40:60), and the Prophet peace be upon him said du'a is worship itself, in Abu Dawud and Tirmidhi. Scholars describe three possible answers: the thing asked for, something equal or better kept back for later, or a harm turned away. He also warned against impatience, saying a servant is answered as long as he does not say I asked and was not answered, in Bukhari and Muslim.

istighfar.s: Asking Allah for forgiveness, usually in the words astaghfirullah.
istighfar.l: The Qur'an links it to relief and provision, quoting Nuh telling his people to seek forgiveness of their Lord (Qur'an 71:10). The Prophet peace be upon him, already promised forgiveness for what preceded and what would follow (Qur'an 48:2), said he sought forgiveness a hundred times a day, in Muslim. Istighfar is the request; tawbah is the turn. They are usually done together, though a person can ask for pardon before they have managed to leave the sin.

tawbah.s: Turning back to Allah from a sin: stopping it, regretting it, and resolving not to return.
tawbah.l: The Qur'an calls for a sincere turning, tawbatan nasuha (Qur'an 66:8). Scholars list the conditions as leaving the sin, regretting it, resolving not to repeat it, and, where a person's right was taken, returning it or seeking their pardon. The Prophet peace be upon him said every child of Adam errs, and the best of those who err are those who repent, in a report collected by Tirmidhi. Falling again does not cancel the earlier repentance; it calls for another one.

inabah.s: Turning to Allah as a settled direction of life, not only as a return after one sin.
inabah.l: The Qur'an commands, turn to your Lord and submit to Him (Qur'an 39:54). Writers on the heart place inabah a step past tawbah: tawbah leaves a wrong behind, inabah keeps facing Him afterwards, in ease as well as in trouble. The picture in the root is of returning again and again to the same place.

muhasabah.s: Taking account of yourself: a regular, honest review of what you did and why.
muhasabah.l: The Qur'an tells each soul to look at what it has sent ahead for tomorrow (Qur'an 59:18), and a well known saying attributed to Umar ibn al-Khattab is to call yourselves to account before you are called to account. Scholars describe it as a short daily session rather than a long anxious one, done before the deed to check the intention and after it to check the result. It is a tool, and like any tool a scrupulous person can overuse it.

muraqabah.s: Living with the awareness that Allah sees you, at the moment you are acting.
muraqabah.l: The Qur'an says He is nearer to a person than his jugular vein (Qur'an 50:16), and that He is ever a watcher over you (Qur'an 4:1). It is the practical side of ihsan as the Prophet peace be upon him defined it to Jibril: worship Allah as though you see Him, and if you do not see Him, then He sees you, in Bukhari and Muslim. Muhasabah looks back at the deed. Muraqabah stands inside it.

zuhd.s: Holding the world loosely: having a thing in your hand without letting it into your heart.
zuhd.l: The Prophet peace be upon him told a man to be indifferent to the world and Allah would love him, and to be indifferent to what people own and people would love him, in a report collected by Ibn Majah. Scholars are clear that zuhd is not poverty and not refusing what is lawful; several Companions were wealthy. It is the willingness to lose a thing without losing yourself along with it.

wara.s: Caution that leaves what is unclear, in order to stay safe from what is forbidden.
wara.l: The Prophet peace be upon him said the lawful is clear and the unlawful is clear, and between them are doubtful matters, and whoever avoids them has protected his religion, in Bukhari and Muslim. He also said to leave what makes you uneasy for what does not, in a report collected by Tirmidhi. Wara' works one step further out than taqwa, in the grey band. It becomes a problem only when it turns into suspicion of everything and everyone.

qanaah.s: Being satisfied with enough, so that what you do not have stops taking up room.
qanaah.l: The Prophet peace be upon him said a person has succeeded who submitted, was given just enough, and was made content by Allah with what He gave him, in Muslim. He also said richness is not having many possessions, but richness of the soul, in Bukhari and Muslim. Qana'ah is not a ban on ambition or on earning. It is the removal of the ache that no amount answers.

hilm.s: Forbearance: the strength to stay calm and unhurried when you have every right to react.
hilm.l: The Prophet peace be upon him told al-Ashajj of Abd al-Qays that he had two qualities Allah loves, hilm and unhurriedness, in Muslim. The Qur'an describes the answer to a rough word as repelling with what is better (Qur'an 41:34). Hilm is not weakness and it is not indifference. The person is fully able to strike back and takes the slower road.

afw.s: Pardon: dropping a wrong you are owed, without the other person having to earn it.
afw.l: The Qur'an asks whether you would not love Allah to forgive you, in the middle of telling a wronged man to pardon (Qur'an 24:22), and says the reward of the one who pardons and reconciles is with Allah (Qur'an 42:40). Scholars distinguish 'afw, letting the debt go, from safh, letting the resentment go with it. The Prophet peace be upon him said Allah only increases a servant in honour for pardoning, in Muslim.

rahmah.s: Mercy: the disposition to spare, relieve and be gentle, in Allah first and in people after.
rahmah.l: The Qur'an says His mercy encompasses all things (Qur'an 7:156), and that the Prophet peace be upon him was sent as a mercy to the worlds (Qur'an 21:107). He said the merciful are shown mercy by the Most Merciful, and told his companions to be merciful to those on earth so that the One in the heaven would be merciful to them, in a report collected by Abu Dawud and Tirmidhi. Rahmah in a person is not softness of opinion. It is the reflex to relieve someone when you could have walked past.

adab.s: Good manner in a specific situation: the right way to sit, speak, eat, enter, and ask.
adab.l: Where akhlaq names the character underneath, adab names the outward form it takes here and now, and most of it was taught by example. Classical scholars wrote whole books on it, such as al-Bukhari's al-Adab al-Mufrad. Some adab is fixed by the Sunnah, such as eating with the right hand, and some varies with place and custom, which is why a practice can be good manners in one country and odd in another.

akhlaq.s: Character: the settled dispositions a person acts from before they have time to think.
